activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: In countries with low death rates, a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman is needed to replace the population without migration.
story:
The map spread across the picnic table kept trying to fold itself, and Jonathan weighted its corners with a thermos and two river stones. It was not a road map but a printout Ms. Friedman had brought on the trip, a population pyramid for their country, bars widening near the middle and thinning toward the bottom like a tree narrowing at the roots. Their assignment, due the last week before summer, was to look at the shape and say what the country would need more of in thirty years: schools or nursing homes. Jonathan had assumed the answer would be obvious. Three days of camping had taught him that nothing Ms. Friedman assigned was ever obvious.

"Look at the bottom rungs," Annabel said, leaning over his shoulder with her mug of instant cocoa. "They're shrinking. That's fewer kids every year, right?" Around them the campsite smelled of woodsmoke and the cold mineral breath of the river, and somewhere behind the tent Leona was arguing with a camp stove that refused to light.

Jonathan traced the bars with one finger, the way Ms. Friedman had shown them in the classroom before the trip, though she had refused to say what any of it meant. "Fewer kids now means fewer parents later," he said slowly, "and fewer parents means even fewer kids after that. It folds forward." He had read an article on the bus up, something about the birth rate falling below two children per woman, and he had shrugged at it, because two sounded like exactly enough. Two people have two children. The numbers replace themselves. It had the tidy sound of a truism, the kind of thing that is repeated until nobody checks it.

Leona abandoned the stove and came over, wiping her hands on her shorts. "You're doing the face," she said. "The face you do in math when the answer is too neat."

"It is too neat," Jonathan said. He told them about the article, and about his assumption, and then found himself stuck on it, turning the arithmetic over the way he turned a stone to see the wet side. "Two for two. Why isn't that steady?"

Annabel counted on her fingers, half joking, and then stopped joking. "Not everyone has kids," she said. "And not everyone even can. Some people don't make it to having kids at all."

Leona sat down on the bench across from him. "So two per woman isn't two per family that actually happens." Jonathan felt something shift, the way a knot gives way all at once after you have been picking at it. He found the article again on his phone, one thin bar of signal surviving at the edge of the campsite, and scrolled until the number surfaced: in countries with low death rates, a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman was needed to replace the population without migration. Two point one. The extra tenth was not padding, not a rounding error; it was the gap between the arithmetic on paper and the arithmetic of actual lives.

"That's it," he said. "That's why the pyramid narrows at the bottom even though everyone's having 'two kids.' The whole country is running below the line." He looked at the shape again and saw it differently now, not a tree but a wave moving up the page, a wide middle section that would age in place, decade by decade, into the top of the chart. "So in thirty years we're not choosing between schools and nursing homes. It's nursing homes, and then the question is who staffs them, because there are fewer people behind the wave."

"You sound like a pamphlet," Leona said, but she was looking at the map too, and her voice had gone quiet.

Ms. Friedman came down from her site at dusk to collect the printouts, and Jonathan told her the 2.1 figure and what he thought it meant for the assignment. She listened with her hands in her jacket pockets and the firelight making her glasses into small orange squares. "Could be," she said. "Or migration could change the shape before the wave arrives. Or policy. You've read one pyramid and one article." She rolled up the map and tapped it once against the table edge. "The honest answer includes the part you can't see yet." He wanted to argue, and then did not, because she was describing exactly the seam he could feel in his own reasoning, the place where the numbers ran out and guessing began. Earlier that spring he had written a scathing margin note in his textbook about a chapter that hedged everything, and he remembered it now with a small heat of embarrassment; caution had looked like cowardice from the outside.

Later, after the fire had burned down to a red skeleton and the others had gone to their tents, Jonathan sat with his notebook and drew the pyramid from memory, bars tapering at the bottom, and beside it he wrote the number and then, underneath, a question he could not close off: what fills the space under the missing children? He could cauterize the question, seal it with the cleanest answer and hand it in, or he could leave it open and write the assignment around the hole. The river kept on past the campsite, indifferent and steady, and he underlined the question twice and put the notebook away, zipping the tent against the cold.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Under the US Credit CARD Act of 2009, card statements must show how long it would take to pay off the balance by making only the minimum payment.
story:
The envelope had his name on it, which was the strange part. Grayson had co-signed nothing, bought nothing, wanted nothing from a bank, and yet here was a piece of mail addressed to him at the kitchen table, between the fruit bowl and his half-finished physics homework. He slid a thumb under the flap. Inside was a credit card with his name embossed on it, and a letter congratulating him on being an authorized user on his mother's account, effective immediately.

He set the card on the table like a small dead animal and went back to finding the coefficient of friction. He lasted four minutes.

His mother came in carrying groceries and saw it lying there. "Oh good, it came. I put you on the card for emergencies. Car breaks down, you need a tow, that kind of thing." She said it lightly, the way she said most things since the divorce, as if lightness were a table leg propping up the rest of the house.

"What counts as an emergency?" he asked.

"Use your judgment," she said, which was her answer to everything lately, and he noticed she didn't expatiate the way she used to, back when there were two incomes and she had the energy for long, amused lectures about compound nouns or the history of jazz. Now her sentences had shortened, as if she were conserving them.

The first statement arrived three weeks later, addressed to his mother but cc'd, in a sense, to him, since he was the one home at four o'clock with nothing to do but open mail. He sat at the kitchen table with a glass of milk and read it like a novel. Balance: six hundred forty dollars, mostly groceries and a car repair. Minimum payment due: twenty-five dollars. And then, in a box near the bottom, in type so small he had to pull the lamp closer, a line he read three times to be sure he had it right.

If he made only the minimum payment each month, the balance would take eleven years to pay off.

He put the statement down and looked at the window, where the neighbor's cat was sitting on the fence post like a small gray accountant. Eleven years. He would be twenty-seven. He would have a degree, possibly a job, possibly an apartment, and somewhere in the background of all of it, this grocery bill from October would still be breathing.

When his mother got home he slid the statement across the table. "Did you see this part?"

She read it standing, one hand still on her coat. "Eleven years," she said. Not a question.

"That's the box they have to put on there now," said Ms. Chea from the doorway, holding a casserole dish she was forever delivering; the two households had a kind of open border. "CARD Act, 2009." She set the dish on the counter and did not say anything else, which was one of her better qualities.

Grayson looked at the number again. Twenty-five dollars a month for eleven years. He did the arithmetic twice on the back of his physics homework. Twenty-five times twelve times eleven was three thousand three hundred dollars. For six hundred forty dollars of groceries and a water pump. The difference, he understood slowly, was interest, the price of borrowing, the meter that keeps running while you drive.

He also had a savings account. He found his own statement in the folder where he kept his pay stubs from the hardware store, and there it was, a line he had never paid attention to: interest earned, one dollar and twelve cents. He'd saved four hundred dollars mowing lawns and stocking shelves, and the bank was paying him for it. Not much. Slightly more than nothing. But running in the opposite direction, the same mechanism, the meter ticking in his favor this time. It was almost elegant, the way the same principle pushed one way when you owed and the other way when you owned, and he felt something shift in how he thought about money, not a seismic collapse of worldview exactly, more like a door opening onto a hallway he'd walked past a thousand times.

At school the next day he told Elina about the eleven years, expecting her to be as stunned as he'd been. She wasn't.

"My mom's been paying minimums on the same card since I was nine," she said. They were in the cafeteria, and she stabbed her fork into the lasagna without much conviction. "Janelle says her parents pay the whole thing every month. Like, the entire balance. That's a whole different life, apparently."

"So which is normal?"

"Neither of them thinks they're the weird one." She shrugged. "Janelle's family also has a cabin."

That was the thing he couldn't resolve, walking home. It was easy to say the bank was a predator and the fine print a trap, but his mother wasn't a fool; she was a person whose hours had been cut and whose alternator had died anyway, and the card had fed them in a week when nothing else would have. Calling the borrowing a mistake felt like calling a splint a mistake because the leg was broken. At the same time, eleven years was eleven years, and three thousand dollars for six hundred forty was not a metaphor. He could hold both ideas. He could not make them sit down together.

That evening he put the card back in the drawer where his mother kept it, then took it out again and left it on the kitchen table, face up, where she'd see it when she came in. He'd written on a sticky note and pressed it to the counter beside the milk: I'll pay the water pump part, $180. From savings.

His mother read it while he pretended to study. She looked at the note, then at the statement, then at him, for longer than the note really required.

"Your savings took you two summers," she said.

"I know."

She sat down across from him and tapped the card once with her finger, the way you'd tap a chess piece you were deciding about. "Twenty-five more a month, from me," she said. "We cut the eleven years down to something reasonable."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
story:
Thomas got to the coffee shop eleven minutes early, which he decided was four minutes too many, so he walked around the block once and came back in at seven minutes early, which still left him standing at the counter with nothing to order behind him yet.

He had texted Kayla an hour before, asking whether arriving early looked desperate. She had replied with a voice memo, which he played in the parking lot with the volume low. "Okay, so, random thing, but I read about this," Kayla said. "There's a study, 2018, by Erica Boothby and colleagues. They called it the liking gap. After a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. Both people. Like, everyone's walking around sure it went worse than it did." Then she said, "You're going to be fine, Thomas," and the memo ended.

Gabriella arrived at two minutes past the hour, shaking rain off her jacket. "The bus," she said. "I'm sorry. It sat at the stop by the bank for, I swear, a full minute with the doors closed."

"That's fine. I just got here." He had been there for nine minutes, and he had already rearranged the sugar dispenser twice.

They ordered. She got a flat white and he got the same thing even though he had been planning on drip coffee, because it seemed easier to say "same as her" than to have two different drinks on the table. They took the corner booth by the window, where the glass fogged at the edges.

The first stretch went badly, in the way first stretches do. He asked about her classes and she said she was doing marine biology, and he asked what that meant, and she said it meant a lot of time kneeling in mud looking at littoral stuff, whatever lived along the shore, crabs and algae and things that could survive being flooded and dried out twice a day. He said that sounded nice, and she asked what his major was, and he said probably philosophy, and she said "Oh," in a tone he couldn't read, and then there was a silence in which he drank too-hot coffee and burned the roof of his mouth.

The silence made him nervous enough to start talking, and the talking made it worse. He began to explain a seminar argument about relativism, how the claim that all truth was relative might itself be only relatively true, and he could hear himself building toward something long, something with premises and a turn. Kayla had once told him he tended to pontificate when he was scared, and he had objected, and she had said the objection itself ran four minutes. He stopped mid-sentence.

"Sorry," he said. "I lecture when I'm nervous."

Gabriella put her cup down. "You're nervous?"

"A little. Yes."

"I made my little brother wait outside with the dog until the bus came," she said, "so I'd have something to do with my hands when I got here. I was going to pet the dog if the table went quiet. He's a very patient dog."

Thomas laughed, and after that the booth got easier. She told him about the tide pools she'd sampled in June, how the crabs all faced the same direction in the current, and he told her about failing his driving test for rolling through a stop sign at two miles an hour, and she said that was technically legal in her heart. They stayed for a second round. When they stood up, the table had a ring of water under his cup and a smaller one under hers, and he thought, distantly, that this counted as evidence of something.

Then he walked home, and somewhere around the bridge over the drainage canal the replay started. The "Oh." The burned mouth. The aborted relativism speech, which now sounded, in memory, worse than if he'd finished it. He had said "same as her" to the cashier like a man with no opinions of his own. She had petted the dog instead of looking at him, probably. By the time he reached his street he had composed and deleted three texts, each one either too eager or too casual, and he had concluded that she had tolerated the afternoon the way you tolerate a dentist.

He sat on the front step instead of going in. He took out his phone and played Kayla's memo again, the part about underestimating. It occurred to him that the study couldn't prove anything about this particular afternoon, that treating it as a rule he could apply was exactly the kind of move his philosophy professor would have dismantled in a paragraph. The gap was what people usually did, on average, and Gabriella was not an average, she was a person who had knelt in mud all June. He couldn't know. But he also couldn't know the other way, and he had spent the last mile treating his worst reading as the only one. That wasn't rigor. That was just the crab facing the current because it was easier.

He typed: "Thanks for today. I had a good time, in case that wasn't obvious. I got the same drink as you because I panicked at the counter."

Her reply came while he was still holding the phone. "It wasn't obvious. I spent the bus ride home convinced you were going to change your major to get away from me."

He read it twice. Then he wrote back, "There's a tide pool thing at the aquarium in March. Do you want to go and tell me what everything is?"

"Only if you don't lecture me about crabs," she said. "Deal," he said, out loud, to the step.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Congress can override a US president's veto with a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate.
story:
The bus smelled of orange peel and hand sanitizer, and Chase had the foldout schedule Ms. Gauthier had printed, now soft at the creases from being opened and shut the whole ride. He wanted one thing from the day: to stand in the chamber while a bill was actually being debated, not watch a video about it, not colour in a worksheet. His civics grade was fine. His understanding was not. Somewhere between "a bill is introduced" and "it becomes law," the whole process had desiccated in his mind into a list of vocabulary words, and today he intended to soak it back into something real.

Ammar had an angle of his own. He'd been tracking a bill in Congress for weeks, one that would fund repairs to the water system in the town where his grandmother lived, and three days ago the president had vetoed it. He sat across the aisle from Chase, phone out, scrolling through the vote record, and he didn't look up when Ms. Gauthier told them to put the phones away, only angled the screen toward the window as if checking the weather.

The capitol was colder than outside, all stone and echo. A legislative aide named only as "the aide" on their badges walked them past the offices where drafts got marked up, past the committee room where a row of chairs faced a long table and a stenographer's machine waited with its keys exposed like teeth. "This is where they take a bill apart," the aide said. "Line by line. Amendments, testimony, all of it, before it ever reaches the floor." Chase copied that into his notebook, not because it would be tested but because he liked the idea of a place built specifically for taking ideas apart.

Then the floor, and the debate, which was not what he had pictured. Two members argued about a clause in a transportation bill, one of them bellicose, leaning over the rostrum, jabbing a finger at the text, the other flat and patient, letting the anger spend itself before answering. The clerk read amendments. A vote was called, names read alphabetically, and the tally appeared on a board above the doors. The bill moved on to its third reading, one step closer to the governor's signature, which the aide called assent, and Chase wrote that word down too.

It was on the wide stone steps afterward, waiting for the bus, that Ammar finally spoke about the veto. "Two hundred and sixty," he said. "That's what the House got. It needed two hundred and ninety." He said it quietly, the way people report scores of games their team lost.

Chase did the arithmetic in his head, and then did it again because the first answer seemed too clean. "Wait," he said. "Two-ninety is two-thirds of the House. So they didn't clear the override there." He looked at the voting record on Ammar's phone, scrolling to the Senate column, where the count stopped before it should have. "They never even got to the Senate."

"Because it was already dead in the House," Ammar said. "Doesn't matter what the Senate would have done."

Chase sat down on the step, ignoring the cold coming up through the stone. He thought about the chamber he had just left, the clerk reading names one by one, each vote a person deciding in a single second. He had assumed a veto was the end of something, a door closing. Now he saw it was more like a raise: the bill's price had doubled, from half the votes to two-thirds, in both the House and the Senate, and this bill simply couldn't pay it. But the two chambers were not the same place. A bill could fail its two-thirds in one and clear it in the other, and Chase realized he had been thinking about Congress as one animal when it was two, each with its own arithmetic.

"So it's over," Ammar said. It wasn't quite a question, and Chase was honest enough not to pretend it was. "For this bill," he said. "Someone can draft it again. Introduce it next session, start over through committee, the whole thing. It happens."

Ammar was quiet, and Chase let him be quiet, because he understood that a process could be fair and still feel like a machine. His civics textbook called the veto override a check, a balance, words that belonged on a diagram. On the steps it was a number of grandmothers who would keep boiling their water, and a number of votes that had come up short by thirty people each deciding, in a single second, that it wasn't theirs to fix.

The late-afternoon light had gone long and golden across the lawn, and Chase watched a groundskeeper dragging a hose toward the dried flowerbeds by the walkway, the spray arcing and falling. He had started the day wanting to see the machine. He had seen it, and it ran exactly as described, drafting and committee and debate and votes, and it had still produced a defeat that nobody in particular was responsible for.

Ammar stood, put the phone in his pocket, and looked back up at the dome. "When they redraft it," he said, "I'm writing to every one of those thirty."

Ms. Gauthier called the roll from the bottom of the steps, and Chase folded his notebook around the pencil and jogged down toward the bus.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech; it does not by itself stop a private employer or private company from restricting speech.
story:
The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and cold coffee, and the folding tables had been pushed against the bleachers to make room for the polling machines. Mia sat in the hallway outside with her legal brief facedown on her lap, because the case had stopped making sense to her somewhere between the majority opinion and her own notes. Her team was here to canvass voters for the school bond, but really she was here because Ms. Silva had said the polling station was the one place in town where every kind of person walked through one door, and Mia needed every kind of person if she was going to argue both sides of Tinker v. Des Moines convincingly enough to survive Monday's mock court.

Emaan came down the hall holding two sample ballots and a granola bar he had no intention of eating. "The guy at table three wants to expatiate on property taxes," he said. "He's been going for ten minutes. I couldn't get away."

"You could have," Mia said. "You stayed because you like it."

"I stayed because he's a registered voter and I'm a volunteer with a clipboard." Emaan dropped into the chair beside her. "What's the brief doing out here? You're supposed to be charming senior citizens."

She turned the pages over, then gave up and turned them back. "I have to argue that the school was right to suspend the kids for wearing the armbands, and then an hour later argue that the school was wrong. Same case, both sides. And I keep finding arguments that sound good until I say them out loud, and then they collapse."

"Like which ones?"

"Like, the school represents order, the students represent dissent, somebody has to win. That sounds like a principle until you ask who decides what order means." She rubbed her eyes. "Ms. Silva keeps saying the point isn't to win. The point is to be able to hold both sides honestly. I don't know what that feels like yet."

A boy from her civics class, a sophomore named Brianne had recruited for the mock court's second team, came out of the gym looking heated. "They deleted my whole thread," he said to no one and then to everyone. "Four hundred posts, gone. That's a free speech violation. First Amendment. I'm going to argue it Monday."

Emaan didn't even look up from his clipboard. "The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech," he said. "Your website isn't the government."

"So? It's censorship."

"It's a private company restricting speech on its own platform. The First Amendment doesn't stop a private company from doing that, and it doesn't stop a private employer either." Emaan shrugged, as if this were the smallest fact he carried. "Take it up with their terms of service."

The boy argued for another minute, then went back inside, and Mia sat very still, because something had just moved in her head like a door opening onto a room she hadn't known was there. She had been thinking of free speech as one flat thing, a shield you either held or didn't. But the shield only faced one direction. It faced the state. A principal was the state. A website was not. Which meant the armband case was never only about whether speech mattered; it was about who was doing the restricting, and that question came first, before any argument about order or dissent could even begin. She wrote in the margin of her brief, who is the actor, and underlined it twice.

That night she drafted a message to Brianne, who had swapped onto the judges' panel and could not coach her without a conflict of interest, though she could, in Brianne's own words, receive mail. Mia wrote it out on paper first, then typed it out. "I've been treating the First Amendment like a wall around all speech everywhere. It's not. It's a wall around the government's reach, and everything outside it is a different question, maybe a harder one. So Monday I'll argue the school had the power to suspend, because schools are the government acting, and then I'll argue the power was misused, and both arguments will be true at the same time. What I still can't figure out is whether that's a real position or just a way of not choosing. Tell me if it's specious. I'd rather know now than on Monday."

Brianne's reply came before breakfast, short the way her messages always were: "Not specious. Uncertain. Those are different things. Judges can smell the difference. Also, the guy with the property taxes is asking for you by name. He wants to convert you."

Monday morning came, and the mock courtroom was the library with the tables rearranged, Ms. Silva presiding in her reading glasses. Mia stood for her first argument and made the case for the school, and it went well, and then she stood again and took it all apart, and that went well too, and afterward Brianne leaned over the bench and said, "Which one did you believe?"

"Both," Mia said. "Ask me again after the real ones."

Ms. Silva tapped her gavel, a stapler actually, against the desk and called the next case. Mia gathered her brief, saw the margin note, who is the actor, and folded the pages around it like a letter she was keeping.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Charles David Keeling of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography began regular carbon dioxide measurements on Mauna Loa, Hawaii, in March 1958; the resulting graph is called the Keeling Curve.
story:
Daniel had been standing in front of the climate exhibit for eleven minutes when Stephan found him, which was long enough for the security guard by the pendulum to start giving him the look reserved for people who might try to touch something. "You're supposed to be helping me," Stephan said, "not communing with the wall."

"It's my presentation," Daniel said. "Ms. Santoso wants me to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat, and then read that graph, the carbon dioxide one. The rising sawtooth line." He pointed at the curve printed on the panel, climbing and dipping, climbing and dipping, like a staircase drawn by someone with a steady hand and a nervous disposition. The dips bothered him. If carbon dioxide was rising, why did it fall every year, and why did nobody explain that part?

Sonny arrived carrying three museum cafeteria cookies balanced on a napkin, which he distributed with the gravity of a man performing a sacrament. "It's photosynthesis," Sonny said, mouth already full. "The whole northern hemisphere has summer, plants inhale, the line drops. Then winter, plants exhale, the line goes back up. It's like the planet breathing."

"That's the earth, not the greenhouse part," Stephan said. "He needs the greenhouse part first. Radiation comes in, hits the ground, comes back out as heat, and the gases in the air absorb the outgoing heat and send some of it back down. More gas, more heat kept." Stephan had written this on his hand in pen during last period, and it was smudged beyond archaeology.

"It's a band," Daniel said slowly, and both of them looked at him. "Not a wall. The gases don't block the sunlight coming in, they catch the heat going out. So the earth's warmer underneath a thinner and thinner blanket being made thicker." He wasn't sure the blanket was his phrase or something Ms. Santoso had said in October that he was only now excavating, but it fit, the way a good fit does, without any of the pieces requiring him to lie.

Then he turned back to the graph, because the graph was the actual assignment, and here he hit the wall Stephan's hand had prefigured. The exhibit called the rising line something, a specific name, and Daniel could not find the station. He squinted at the small print. "It says Scripps Institution of Oceanography," he said, "but I know there was a station. An actual place where a guy measured this, starting way back, before anyone cared." He had read it two nights ago at one in the morning and let it dissolve into sleep, and now the knowledge sat somewhere unreachable, like a word on the tip of the tongue that refuses to arrive on principle.

Sonny leaned over the cookie napkin. "Try the interactive screen." The screen, after a petulant thirty seconds of loading, offered a timeline. Daniel typed in oceanography, then carbon dioxide, then, on Sonny's suggestion, volcano, because he had a vague memory of a volcanic peak. Hawaii came up. Mauna Loa. March 1958, and a scientist, Charles David Keeling, who began taking regular measurements of carbon dioxide there, at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography's station, month after month, until the numbers made the line.

"That's it," Daniel said. He copied the details into his notebook, transcribing them twice because his handwriting degraded when he was excited. "Charles David Keeling, Mauna Loa, Hawaii, March 1958. And they named the graph after him."

"It's called the Keeling Curve," said Sonny, reading off the screen, in the tone of a man announcing a winner.

Daniel stood still for a moment. He thought about the version of himself two nights ago, skimming, letting the name slide past, and the version now, who had it cold. Somewhere between them, in a museum with his friends and their cheap cookies, the presentation had become something he could actually give, though he still wasn't sure he could answer the question of why one man's patience mattered more than a hundred conferences. The pendulum swung behind them with its soft, ticking diminuendo, counting out the seconds it had been counting all day, indifferent to who was watching.

"Okay," he said. "Thursday. I open with the breathing planet, then the band, then the curve." He closed the notebook. "Sonny, you're the demo."

"Am I the blanket?"

"You're the blanket."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: New Zealand was the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting, when its government and Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990 on a target range of 0 to 2 percent.
story:
Zoe's mother had taped the assignment to the fridge: prepare a five-minute explanation of how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation, and be ready to present it to the seminar without notes. Zoe sat at the kitchen table with a bowl of cereal going soft, a textbook open to a chapter with too many arrows in its diagrams, and her phone face down like a defendant refusing to testify.

"Explain it to the wall," said Lyra, who had come over ostensibly to study chemistry but was currently lying on the kitchen floor with her feet up on a chair. "If you can explain it to the wall, you can explain it to anyone."

"The wall doesn't ask follow-up questions," Zoe said. "The wall doesn't say, wait, but why does borrowing less make prices stop rising?" She picked up her phone, found Eliane's contact, and typed: You're my wall for the next ten minutes. Then she called out to the ceiling, mostly to hear the shape of the words: "Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, so people and businesses take out fewer loans, so they spend less, so sellers can't keep raising prices."

"Say the last part again," Lyra said from the floor, "but like you believe it."

"That's the problem. I believe all the parts and I don't believe the sentence."

A message came back from Eliane: Fine, but the wall charges by the minute. Zoe grinned and typed her draft in three long texts, the way she would say it aloud. Eliane's reply was characteristically effusive, three exclamation points and a heart, which Zoe distrusted on principle; effusiveness from Eliane usually meant she was being kind rather than convinced. Then came the follow-up: Ok but one thing. Has it always been like this? Like, did central banks always have a number they were aiming at? Ms. Horváth said something about that once and I forgot it.

Zoe frowned at the screen. It was exactly the kind of question the seminar teacher loved, the kind that made her prepared five minutes evaporate. She went looking, keyboard clicks filling the kitchen, and found the answer faster than she expected, which made her suspicious enough to check it twice.

"Lyra. Guess which country did inflation targeting first."

"America," Lyra said, "because America does everything first."

"New Zealand. It wasn't the Fed, it wasn't the Bank of England, it was New Zealand. The government and the Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990, and the target range was 0 to 2 percent." She said it twice, testing the weight of it. "Nineteen ninety. That's after my mom finished university. It's newer than my mom's degree."

"That can't be right," Lyra said, sitting up. "Banks are old. Banks have beards."

"Central banks are old. The target is young." Zoe read the page again, the numbers sitting there plain as a bus schedule. She turned back to her messages and typed it out for Eliane, every part, because Eliane would absolutely ask for the range and Zoe refused to be caught without it. Then she sat with the strange little fact, rolling it around. The agreement hadn't floated down from economics heaven; someone had sat in a room in Wellington and decided to codify a promise into an actual number. Which meant the whole apparatus her textbook drew with arrows had been built by people, recently, on purpose, and could presumably be built differently.

"That actually helps," she said slowly. "Because if the target is a choice, then the interest rate is the tool for hitting the choice. Nobody's raising rates for fun. They're raising rates to steer toward a number somebody picked."

Lyra pointed a fork at her. "There. Say it exactly like that tomorrow."

"It's still a chain of so's," Zoe said. "So rates go up, so loans shrink, so spending cools, so price rises slow down. I can say the chain. What I can't do is prove the chain to a skeptic, and we have at least two skeptics in that seminar and one of them is Eliane."

Eliane's next message arrived: Wait, stagflation though. Doesn't high inflation sometimes come WITH a bad economy? Then raising rates makes the bad part worse? Zoe groaned aloud and put her forehead on the table.

"I was almost done," she told the table.

"That's the good question," Lyra said, not unkindly. "The one that doesn't have a neat answer. You could just say that part out loud, you know. Say, here's where it gets hard."

Zoe lifted her head. On the notepad where her outline lived, she drew a line under her last point and wrote, in smaller letters, and here's what I still can't explain. She looked at it, then at the time, then at her phone, where Eliane had sent a single question mark.

"Come over," Zoe typed. "Bring snacks. We're going to break my presentation and then put it back together."

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: The Higgs boson discovery on July 4, 2012 was announced only after two separate CERN detector teams, ATLAS and CMS, independently found the same new particle.
story:
Wyatt had wanted the junior docent badge since October, when he'd seen a boy about his age lead a tour through the physics hall and get thanked, actually thanked, by strangers. Now it was March, the museum had chosen two finalists instead of one, and the coordinator, Ms. Clarke, had explained the arrangement with the enthusiasm of someone reading a parking notice. He and Kassandra would each answer visitor questions for one afternoon. Whoever did better got the badge. Kassandra wanted it just as much, which was the inconvenient part, because she was also the only person here he could talk to.

The physics hall sat between the butterfly biome and a gift shop, so the air smelled faintly of humid greenery and microwave popcorn, a combination Wyatt suspected no one had planned. He spent the first hour pointing at the cloud chamber and saying "cosmic rays" with reasonable confidence. Then a man in a grey windbreaker stopped at the particle physics wall and squinted at a photograph of a cavernous underground chamber, all scaffolding and cables.

"Why'd they build two of these?" the man asked. "Seems like a lot of money for a backup."

Wyatt looked at the photo. There were two detectors, and he knew the project was CERN, and he knew, vaguely, that something called the Higgs boson had been discovered on July 4, 2012, because the date was printed in large letters beside a cake in the photo, someone at CERN apparently having a sense of occasion. Beyond that, his mind produced a soft blue blank.

"Redundancy," he said. "In case one breaks."

Kassandra had drifted over from the cloud chamber, and he could feel her not looking at him, which was its own kind of looking. "You're prognosticating," she said quietly, once the man had turned back to the wall. "You're predicting what the answer should be instead of, you know, reading the answer."

"I wasn't prognosticating. I was estimating."

"You were guessing with a suit on."

The exhibit text ran along the bottom of the wall in small type, and Wyatt crouched to read it, pretending this had been his plan all along. The text said what he should have known: the discovery of the Higgs boson on July 4, 2012 was announced only after two separate teams, ATLAS and CMS, running independent detectors, found the same new particle. He read it twice. ATLAS and CMS. Not a backup. Two groups of scientists who had built their own machines, gathered their own data, and reached the same conclusion without sharing a lunch table, and only then did anyone stand up in a auditorium and say the word "discovered."

"So it's like doing the experiment twice," he said aloud, mostly to himself.

"With different people," Kassandra said, peering over his shoulder. "Who are allowed to be jealous of each other."

The man in the windbreaker had come back around the case and was standing close enough to have heard the whole exchange. Wyatt braced for the version of this where the visitor explained everything at length, the way his uncle explained tax brackets, but the man only pulled a lanyard out of his collar. It said CERN on it, and under that, a name and the word CMS.

"I worked on CMS," the man said. "ATLAS found it first, actually. By about two hours of press conference scheduling." He smiled at the photo of the cake. "Nobody believed either of us alone."

Ms. Clarke appeared at the end of the hall with her clipboard, wearing the ascetic expression she reserved for evaluating things, and Wyatt realized with a slow drop in his stomach that she had been near enough to hear his first answer, the one about backups. She didn't say anything. She made a mark on the clipboard and moved toward the butterflies.

"Okay," Kassandra said. "That was a disaster."

"That was a physicist."

"A physicist who heard you say it was a backup."

Wyatt straightened up. The right move was obvious: walk over, tell Ms. Clarke he'd gotten it wrong and then gotten it right, and let the badge go to whoever it went to. The wrong move was to stand here and let his guess harden into a story he'd tell later, the one where he'd basically known it all along. He'd watched his father do that with the stock he'd almost bought, prognosticating the past until it came out in his favor.

He found Ms. Clarke by the biome entrance, where blue morphos drifted over a tray of rotting fruit. "I told a visitor the second detector was a backup," he said. "It wasn't. The Higgs was announced on July 4, 2012 only because ATLAS and CMS both found the same new particle, independently. Two separate teams."

Ms. Clarke's pen stopped. She looked at him for a moment, then past him, to where Kassandra was telling the windbreaker man something about the cloud chamber, gesturing with both hands.

"Is she going to correct you next?" Ms. Clarke asked.

"She already did."

Ms. Clarke wrote something, and the butterflies moved in their slow, argumentative circles overhead, and one of them landed on Kassandra's shoulder just as the man started to laugh.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The SAT switched to a digital, adaptive format in the United States in March 2024: how well a student does on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second.
story:
The letter would come by email, which meant it could come at any hour, which meant Chloe had begun to treat her inbox the way her grandmother treated weather, checking it with a calm face and a fast pulse. She sat at the kitchen table with her laptop open and a mug of tea going cold beside her, the pad of her thumb wearing a small grey smudge onto the trackpad. Across the table, Blake was peeling an orange in one long spiral, the kind of pointless skill you develop the year everything else matters too much.

"Refresh it later," Blake said. "They said by Friday. It's Tuesday."

"I'm not refreshing. I'm looking at my SAT score report." She turned the screen a few degrees toward him. "I keep going back to the math section. I thought I bombed it. The second module was brutal, the questions got so hard I ran out of time on the last two, and I left the test center sure I'd have to take it again."

Blake dropped a segment of orange into his mouth and spoke around it. "That's the thing, though. You took it in March, right? The SAT went digital that month. It's adaptive now. How you do on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second one." He reached over and tapped the screen. "Hard questions in module two probably means you did well enough on module one to get the harder set. You weren't failing. You were being challenged."

Chloe looked at him, then at the number on the screen, the number she had already memorized and distrusted. "That's it? Harder means better?"

"That's what the whole thing is built on. Dane figured it out before we tested, in October. He said don't panic if the second half feels worse. I panicked anyway, and then I got my score and it was fine." Blake shrugged, as if this were a small mercy of the system rather than a trick it played on everyone equally.

She sat with that for a moment, turning her mug so the handle faced the window, where the late light was making the caulking along the frame look friable, soft and crumbable, the way old seals go. It was strange to think that the test had already known things about her that she hadn't known herself, that somewhere in a server her first module had quietly circumscribed what the second one would dare to ask. She had walked out of that room certain of failure, and the certainty had been wrong, and the wrongness had lasted for weeks, through the application, the essay she'd rewritten four times, the fee her mother paid without comment while the money sat visibly thin in the account.

"Mr. Yamamoto said something once," she said. "When he came back from his sabbatical. That the hardest problems are the ones you get handed after you've proven you can handle the ones before. I thought he was being a motivational poster about it. But it's literally how the test works now."

"He'd like that. He can put it on the whiteboard."

"He can't. He retired." She pulled the laptop closer and opened her essay, the one about her mother's restaurant and the year the fryer broke and they cooked everything in the one working pan. She read the first paragraph, and for the first time in a month she didn't want to change it. The words were simple because the thing they described had been simple, a small kitchen, an inventory of what still worked, a decision made anyway.

Blake finished the orange and folded the peel into a tight square. "So what happens if it's no?"

"I take a gap term. I work at the restaurant. I apply again with the spring deadline." She said it steadily, and mostly meant it, though she could feel the shape of the other future underneath, the one where the email said no and the no meant something about her rather than about a committee reading two hundred files in a weekend.

The phone on the counter buzzed, and both of them went still, and then it was only her mother, texting that she'd picked up bean sprouts and would Chloe start the rice. Chloe typed back that she would. Then she closed the essay, and before she could think better of it she refreshed the inbox. The message was there, third from the top, the subject line nothing but a capital letter and the name of the college.

"Open it or don't," Blake said, "but if you don't, I'm opening it."

"You wouldn't."

"Chloe. I have been sitting at this table since four o'clock."

She moved the cursor over it. Outside, a bird landed on the fence and then left again, and the rice cooker clicked on by itself, having decided it was time. She clicked.

"Read it out loud," Blake said.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: A blind spot is an area around a car the driver cannot see from the seat, even with mirrors, which is why drivers turn their heads to check before changing lanes.
story:
I was completely calm, which is why my hands were shaking. My father had agreed to this lesson on the condition that we never speak of the mailbox incident, which had never happened, since I had personally resuscitated the mailbox with duct tape and nobody could prove otherwise. He settled into the passenger seat with the expression of a man boarding a ship he suspected was sinking. Behind us, in spirit if not in fact, were Amir and Olive, who had texted me eleven combined messages that morning, ranging from Olive's "you will be fine, statistically" to Amir's "my cousin dented three cars learning, no shame in the lineage."

The car was the family sedan, obstreperous in the way of old machines, the kind that shudders when it wakes up and groans through turns like it's filing a complaint. My father adjusted the mirror on his side, then mine, angling it until the reflection of the street behind us looked, to him, correct. I put my hands at ten and two, because that was the one thing I remembered from the handbook, and pulled out of the driveway with what I considered flawless smoothness. My father braced one hand on the dash. He said nothing, which in his language is a paragraph of praise.

We drove the long loop past the school and the shuttered garden center, and I began to feel that driving was, in fact, easy, and that everyone who had ever failed a road test was simply weak. This is a habit of mine, according to Olive, who keeps a list. I announced that I might take the test early, maybe next month, and my father made a sound like a kettle deciding against boiling.

The problem was the left turn onto Marsh Road. The lane was narrow and a delivery truck sat at the curb, so I eased left to get around it, and it was at that exact moment that I discovered the mirror had been lying to me my whole life. The mirror showed an empty road. The mirror showed sky, distance, freedom. And then a horn, close and furious, and a silver hatchback sliding past on my left, close enough that I could see the driver's mouth forming a word my father would not have appreciated me repeating. I yanked the wheel back, and the sedan and I shuddered to the curb, and I sat there breathing like I'd run a mile.

"That car was there the whole time," I said.

"Yep," my father said.

"In my mirror it was not there."

"Yep," he said again, with the terrible patience of a man who had predicted this. He did not explain. He has a theory that things you find out yourself stay found, whereas things you're told slide off by Friday. So instead he tapped the mirror with one finger and looked at me, waiting, which is his version of a lecture.

And I got it, slowly, the way you get things. There was a zone around the car, a whole area, that I could not see from the driver's seat no matter how the mirrors were aimed. The mirror wasn't lying exactly; it was only telling me about the part of the world it could reach, and the hatchback had been sitting in the unreachable part, perfectly real, perfectly invisible. "So there's a blind spot," I said, and my father nodded once, like a judge. "An area around the car I can't see even with the mirrors." He kept nodding. "That's why you do that thing," I said. "That weird neck thing. You turn your head before you change lanes."

"Before every lane change, every time," he said. "Head turn, then wheel."

This was, I admit, a blow to my theory of natural driving genius. But it was also strangely comforting, the way most true things are. Amir's leitmotif, the joke he deploys at every available occasion, is that the world is mostly stuff you can't see coming, so you might as well check your blind spots where you can. I had always taken it as Amir being Amir, philosophical about failed quizzes and spoiled milk. Now it seemed like actual engineering.

We pulled back out, and I practiced the turn onto Marsh Road four more times, and each time I turned my head before the wheel, an exaggerated swivel, chin to shoulder, like a suspicious owl. The fifth time a car was actually there, a red one, sitting quietly in the invisible zone, and I saw it only because I looked, and I stayed in my lane and let it pass, and my father exhaled the exhale of a man whose ship has, for now, stayed afloat.

The blind spot did not go away with practice, which was the other thing I understood that afternoon. It was permanent, structural, part of the deal. You did not defeat it; you remembered it existed and turned your head, every single time, forever. When I told Olive this later, texting from the driveway with the engine ticking as it cooled, she replied that this was either a metaphor or just good driving, and that she refused to decide which. Amir wrote back a single thumbs up and the words "lineage intact."

I sat in the cooling car a while longer. Tomorrow, I decided, I would drive the loop again, and the next day after that, and eventually I would take the test, head swiveling like it owed me money. There would still be whole regions of the road I couldn't see, and whole stretches of the next few years that no mirror of mine would show me clearly, and the best I could do was keep looking anyway, before every turn, before every change.

My father knocked on the window and held up the duct tape. "You're going to need more of this," he said.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by communication researcher Jeffrey Hall estimated it takes roughly 50 hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
The boxes in Hunter's new room smelled like someone else's basement, which was fair, because until last month they had lived in someone else's basement, namely his. He counted them on Marrow Street, all thirty-one, lined up along a wall the color of weak tea. The movers had been munificent with tape, wrapping even his desk lamp as though it were heirloom crystal, and unwrapping anything now required the patience of an archaeologist. Outside, a sprinkler ticked across a lawn he did not yet have to mow, and somewhere down the block a dog barked twice, then thought better of it.

He had lived in Fenwick for exactly twenty-two days, which he knew because he was keeping a ledger. Not a metaphorical ledger. An actual notebook, blue, spiral-bound, with a column for names and a column for hours. This began the evening Ms. Horváth, his English teacher, had assigned a research paragraph on "a statistic that changed how you see your own life," and Hunter, desperate and curious in equal parts, had typed the word friendship into the library database at nine at night. He found a 2018 study by a communication researcher named Jeffrey Hall, who had estimated that it takes roughly 50 hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. Hunter read the sentence three times, then went downstairs and ate an entire bowl of cereal standing up, feeling like a man who had just been handed the exchange rate for a currency he'd been spending blind his whole life.

The next morning he started the ledger. It was, he admitted, a slightly deranged response. His mother said so, gently, over the last of the cereal. "You can't spreadsheet people, sweetheart." But she said it while alphabetizing the spice rack, so neither of them took the moral high ground. And Hunter had his reasons. In Fenwick he had never once wondered how friendships were made; they had accreted, the way his old town's everything accreted, slowly and without his noticing. Here, everyone already had their people. Here, everything had to be counted, scheduled, pursued on purpose, and the pursuit made him feel like a door-to-door salesman of his own personality.

Judy was the closest to qualifying. She sat behind him in Ms. Horváth's class and had an outré habit of annotating her novels with sticky notes that just said "hm" or "bold choice." After the research paragraph came back with his statistic circled and the comment "so then, is loneliness just arithmetic?", she had leaned over his shoulder, read it, and said, "Fifty hours. That's nothing. That's like two seasons of a show." After that they had started eating lunch together, and Hunter had begun, without shame, tallying. Lunch was 35 minutes. Walking to the parking lot, 6. The day they spent four hours failing to assemble her secondhand bookshelf, which had been sold to her without its crucial dowels and which they eventually propped upright with hardbacks, that was a windfall. By Friday of the third week, Judy's column read 19.4 hours.

The problem, and he knew it was a problem even as he sharpened his pencil, was that the counting had begun to eat the thing counted. He caught himself watching the clock at lunch the way you watch a kettle. When Judy expatiated on the plot of her graphic novel, a speech that took in betrayal, cyclones, and a suspicious ferret, he caught himself calculating whether monologues counted as time together or whether they were more like adjacent solitude. He had a whole debate with himself about it on the walk home, out loud, slightly, which startled a jogger.

It was Emy, the girl from his street with the drum kit in the garage, who flipped the ledger sideways. She had come over because his mother had invited the whole block to a "casual get-together," which featured seven kinds of dip and his mother's anxious trifecta of jokes about the moving truck. Emy, a junior with a talent for showing up where food was, had found Hunter in his room, discovered the notebook under a sandwich, and read the whole thing with the delight of someone finding a stranger's diary. "You wrote down the bookshelf," she said. "Four hours. You wrote down the bookshelf, and next to it, in pen, 'deduct 30 min, mostly silent.'"

"Silence counts," Hunter said. "I decided it counts."

"You decided it counts." She flipped back a page. "It says here you deducted it." She looked at him with an expression that contained, he would think later, an entire competitive career's worth of judgment. Then she said the thing that had not occurred to him, which was simple and slightly devastating: "You've been hanging out with your notebook about Judy more than with Judy." She tore out the page, folded it into a paper football, and flicked it at his head. It bounced off his ear into the dip tray.

He wanted to argue, and found he couldn't, and found also that he was laughing, which complicated the argument further. The truism his grandfather liked, that the best things in life can't be measured, had always struck Hunter as the kind of thing people say when they're bad at spreadsheets. But the study was real too, the hours were real, and somewhere between the two was an actual truth, which was that the 50 hours were a door and not a destination, and that he had been standing at the door, stopwatch raised, instead of walking through it. What stayed uncertain, what he could not make tidy in any column, was whether you could choose to love the person you'd spent the hours on, or whether the hours did the choosing. He suspected the answer was yes, both, in that order and also in reverse, depending on the day.

Monday at lunch he brought the blue notebook and set it in the center of the table between his tray and Judy's. She looked at it with deep suspicion, the way she looked at the word "fetch" in Victorian novels. "Don't panic," Hunter said. "It's a gift." He pushed it across, and when she opened it and saw her own name at the top of a column of small, earnest numbers, she was quiet for a moment, and then she took out a pen and wrote, at the bottom of her page, in her cramped left-slanting hand, "hm." Then she flipped to the first blank page, wrote her name again at the top of a fresh column, and handed it back. "Start over," she said. "I get the ledger this time."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate.
story:
The dressing room smelled the way it always did, like wet wool and orange peels and something no one ever named, and Vincent sat on the bench unlacing his skates for what the schedule on the fridge said was the second-to-last time. He had done the math on the drive over, because that was the kind of thing he did when he didn't want to think about other things. Fourteen skates left if you counted warmups. Then a banquet in the gym with folding chairs and a lasagna that was, by all accounts, interminable.

Jared had been trying to convince everyone for a week that the team should go out with something memorable. "A ritual," he kept saying, as if the word itself settled the matter. "Teams need rituals. It's anthropology." Brady said anthropology was exactly the excuse Jared needed to make people sing in public, and Jared said no, singing was only one option among several, and Brady said that was not reassuring.

The problem, as Vincent understood it, was simpler and worse than any ritual. Three of the seniors, including Jared's brother's old liney, were done after this season. The goalie was moving to Halifax. The whole shape of the thing they had built was about to come apart, and nobody wanted to say so, because saying so in a dressing room was like saying the word "concussion": technically allowed, socially forbidden.

He had found the answer, or something shaped like an answer, in the school library on Tuesday, while pretending to research an essay about the Trans-Canada Highway. Ms. Fitzgerald had shelved a sociology textbook beside the atlas stand, and he had opened it out of boredom, which was how he found most of the important things he knew. There was a chapter about groups. Forming, storming, norming, performing, and then a fifth stage that somebody named Tuckman and a woman named Mary Ann Jensen had added in 1977, after the original four, for when a group's work ends and members separate.

At the last practice, Coach kept the drills short and let them play shinny for the final twenty minutes, which he never did. The ice was soft at the ends and Brady fell twice on the same lazy turn, and everyone laughed, and Brady laughed hardest, which was one of his best qualities. Then the coach blew the whistle and said, "That's the season, gentlemen," and it landed strangely, like a door closing somewhere in a far part of the house.

The party was in Jared's basement, with his mother upstairs providing pizza and a quantity of vegetables nobody touched. Vincent waited until the third pizza, when everyone was loose and loud, then climbed onto the coffee table, which destabilized under him immediately, one leg skating out sideways, so that he delivered his speech from a half-crouch, gripping the curtain rod for balance. "I have prepared remarks," he announced, in his best elocution, which he had practiced in the bathroom mirror and which Brady immediately ruined by saying, "He practiced that voice."

"Groups have stages," Vincent said. "There's forming, storming, norming, performing. And in 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth one, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate." He paused. The goalie had stopped chewing. "We're in that one. Right now. And it has a name, which means it happens to everybody, which means it's not just us being weird about pizza."

For a second nobody said anything, and Vincent worried he had turned a party into a funeral. Then Jared's brother's old liney said, "So we're adjourning," testing the word, and Brady said, "I thought that was what you did to a jury," and the room broke up laughing, and the goalie raised his slice of pizza like a toast to the fifth stage of everything.

Jared got his ritual in the end, though not the one he'd planned. Someone suggested they all sign the goalie's old blocker, the cracked one he'd been meaning to throw out since November, and it went around the basement in a slow circle, each of them crouched over it with a Sharpie, writing things that were mostly insults. Vincent wrote his in the corner where the padding met the plastic: Fifth stage. Not the last one.

Later, walking home with his stick over his shoulder like a rifle in a movie he'd half-seen, Vincent turned it over. He still wasn't sure whether knowing a thing had a name made it easier or just gave the sadness a place to file itself. The goalie would make new friends in Halifax; the seniors would end up on some beer league in six years pretending they'd never left. Probably. He didn't know. The streetlight at the corner buzzed and steadied, and he smacked a pebble all the way across the intersection with the flat of his blade.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: White coat hypertension is when blood pressure reads high in a clinic, often from nervousness, but normal at home, so doctors may check it with home or all-day monitoring.
story:
Wyatt had eleven minutes before the hygienist called Eshan back, which meant eleven minutes to fix the presentation, and the presentation was their grade for Health Sciences, due at 2:40, ninety minutes from now. He sat in the dentist's waiting room with his laptop balanced on his knees, the charger cord snaking to an outlet beneath the magazine rack. The slide on the screen read, in Wyatt's own dead words, "Blood Pressure: Why It Matters." Eshan, beside him with a swollen jaw held in a bag of peas from the front desk, had already pronounced it boring twice.

"It has to have a real case study," Eshan said through the peas. "Mr. Pham said case studies or nothing."

"Mr. Pham teaches chemistry. Why does he care about our health presentation?"

"He cares about anything that isn't a poster." Eshan shifted the peas to his other cheek. "Ask them to take your blood pressure. You're sitting in a medical office. Free data."

Wyatt looked toward the desk, where a machine sat on a small table beside the clipboard stand, a cuff folded over its arm like a sleeping animal. He had never had his taken. The idea enthralled him briefly, the way real instruments enthralled him, the way scales and calipers did, devices that turned a body into numbers. He rolled up his sleeve, slid his arm in, and pressed start while Eshan filmed it for the presentation. The cuff tightened, tightened past comfort, then sighed loose. The screen blinked: 148 over 92.

"That's high," Eshan said, leaning over. "Is that high?"

"It's the top number that... I don't actually know." Wyatt pulled up the chart he'd half-memorized for the presentation and felt his stomach drop. Elevated. High. He was sixteen. He ran cross country, badly but he ran it. He thought of his grandfather's stroke, of the phrase "silent killer" from a website he'd skimmed at one in the morning, and his own pulse began ticking in his ears like something subterranean, a pipe knocking under a floor.

The hygienist appeared with a clipboard and called Eshan's name, and Eshan went back holding his peas, and Wyatt was alone with the number. He tried again. 151 over 94. Higher. He took a third reading with his eyes closed and got 146, and none of this was going onto any slide, because apparently he was dying quietly in a dentist's waiting room while his partner got a root canal. He texted Ilyas, who was already at school setting up the projector: change of plan, might have real problem, will explain. Ilyas replied with a single question mark. The clock over the desk said 1:22. Their presentation was third, after Eshan's own root canal, and the bus that connected this office to the school came at 1:40 or not again until 2:15, which would be cutting the deadline to nothing.

Mr. Pham, meanwhile, was in the office only because his wife had an appointment and he had come to drive her home. He noticed the boy at the blood pressure machine because the boy had now taken four readings in ten minutes and was writing them all down with the grim concentration of someone drafting a will. Mr. Pham recognized him from third-period chemistry, the one who argued about sig figs, an iconoclast in the smallest and most harmless sense, and he came over because a teacher's habits didn't switch off in waiting rooms.

"Mr. Pham," Wyatt said, before any greeting. "If you took your blood pressure right now, in a medical office, and it was high, but you were also really nervous, does the nervousness count? Or is it the high number?"

Mr. Pham glanced at the machine's screen, at the column of figures in Wyatt's notebook. "They have a name for that," he said. "White coat hypertension."

"Which means what, exactly?"

"That's your presentation, not mine." He raised an eyebrow at the clock. "But your dentist would tell you it's when a reading is high in a clinic because of nerves, and normal at home. If it keeps happening, they don't just trust the clinic number. They check with readings at home, or a monitor you wear all day."

Wyatt wrote it down faster than he had written anything all year. High here, from nervousness. Normal at home. Home readings, or all-day monitoring. His hands were shaking, which was either evidence for his theory or a symptom of something worse, and he could not tell the difference, and he hated that he could not tell the difference. The whole point of numbers was that they didn't shake. He had built the presentation around the idea that a reading was a verdict, and now the verdict itself was nervous, and that changed every slide he had.

At 1:38 Eshan came out with a numb half-face and a paper full of instructions, and they ran for the bus, Wyatt carrying the laptop open against his chest, rewriting the second slide as he walked. "New thesis," he said. "The number isn't the story. The story is where you take it." Eshan mumbled something that might have been agreement, peas still pressed to his jaw.

They made the 1:40 with four seconds left. Ilyas texted again: which slide do you want me to pull up first. Wyatt typed, then deleted, then typed again. He would present it as a question, not an answer, his own arm as the case study, the 148 and the uncertainty both on the slide. Then he closed the laptop, wrapped the cuff's remembered squeeze around his wrist, and looked out the window the whole way to school.

"Second slide," he said finally. "Put up the question mark."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: Murmansk, a Russian port north of the Arctic Circle, stays ice-free all year because of warm water carried by the North Atlantic Current.
story:
The map had come from Mr. Sow, folded into eighths and smelling faintly of the noxious camp fuel he used in his stove, and James spread it across the picnic table with the confidence of someone who had read a map before, once, of a subway. It showed the North Atlantic in swirling bands of blue and orange, arrows curling off the coast of Florida like spilled ribbons. The campsite around them was all pine and damp, and the ocean was a four-hour drive away, which struck James as either a flaw in the assignment or proof of Mr. Sow's particular sense of humor. "Gulf Stream," James said, tapping the orange ribbon, as though introduction made them friends.

The assignment was this: each of them had to learn one thing well enough to teach it, and teach it around the fire on the last night. James had chosen ocean currents because it had sounded impressive at the time, and because Mr. Sow had said, in that mild way of his, "That one's harder than it looks." James had assumed this was encouragement. He was, he would later admit, not always right about that sort of thing.

Jameson sat across the table with his own project, a knot-tying display he was assembling with great care, and no interest whatsoever in oceans. Jameson's want was simple and longstanding: he intended to impress Katie, who was arriving Saturday with her father, the coach, and who had once said at a school bonfire that competence was the most underrated quality in a person. Jameson had been building competence ever since, knot by knot. He looped a bowline and cinset it, and said, "You know what you're doing with that thing, right?"

"Obviously," said James, who at that point could locate Florida and, on a good day, Europe.

The trouble arrived on Saturday evening, in the person of Katie herself, who leaned over the map with her rain jacket still dripping and asked the question James had been dreading without knowing it existed. She pointed at the top of the map, at the high gray latitudes, and said, "Last winter my dad was talking about how ships get into Murmansk. It's a Russian port north of the Arctic Circle. Why would ships reach a port that far north in winter? Shouldn't it be frozen solid?" She looked at James with genuine curiosity, and Jameson, watching her watch James, felt something in his chest debilitate his entire knot-tying agenda.

James looked at the map. From the small island of things he actually knew, certain fragments offered themselves. There was the orange ribbon leaving Florida, warm water moving north, and the arrows that continued across the Atlantic toward those same high latitudes where Murmansk sat, defiantly ice-free, according to a fact surfacing in his memory from some documentary watched at 1 a.m. "Murmansk stays ice-free all year," he said slowly, "because warm water carried by the North Atlantic Current reaches it." He traced the arrow with his finger, and the finger arrived where the port was, and the two facts, the ribbon and the port, clicked together in his head with an almost audible sound. "It doesn't freeze. That's the whole point of the map."

Katie's view of this exchange, had anyone recorded it, differed from James's own account, which he gave later around the fire with the flourish of a man who had known the answer all along and had merely been waiting for a worthy audience. In her version, he had gone quiet for a long moment, mouth slightly open, staring at the map like it owed him money, and then said "wait, wait" twice before producing the sentence about warm water and the North Atlantic Current. She had found this, privately, more impressive than fluency would have been. Anyone could recite. Not everyone could be seen putting the pieces together and then stand there honestly saying, "What I still can't figure out is whether the current just doesn't lose its heat by then, or whether something else is going on, and I don't want to guess at you." That required a certain discernment, she thought, the willingness to know the edge of what you knew.

Around the fire, the last night, Mr. Sow turned the map toward the flames so the orange ribbon glowed. Katie fed a stick into the coals and said, "So the warm water goes all that way north, and Murmansk, above the Arctic Circle, never freezes because of it." Jameson, who had finished his knots an hour before and demonstrated them to general applause and to one specific person's, folded his hands behind his head. "You know what else never freezes," he said. "Me. I run cold, Katie. I'm basically ice-free." She looked at him across the fire and said, "Show me the bowline again."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: In Canadian federal elections, an eligible voter who is not on the voters list can register at their assigned polling place on election day.
story:
Robert turned eighteen in March, and when his mother taped the voter information card to the fridge in September, he stood in front of it with a glass of juice and read his own name printed there beside his parents'. Then, on the first Monday after the writ dropped, he came home from school and looked for a card of his own and found nothing.

"So I'm not on the list," he said at dinner, setting his fork down.

His father reached for the salt. "You filled out that form at the DMV when you renewed your health card."

"That was mom, for the address change. I never did one." He had assumed, all summer, that turning eighteen was the operative act, that eligibility flowed into registration the way water finds a drain. Apparently it did not.

His sister, twelve and delighted by any failure of his, said, "So you can't vote. First election and you already can't vote."

He told her to eat her peas. His mother said he could call Elections Canada in the morning, and his father said something about there probably being a deadline, the way there was a deadline for everything, tax forms and passport renewals, and Robert felt the familiar weight of an administrative world designed by people who had never been eighteen and disorganized at the same time. He did not say anything petulant, though the sentence formed itself fully in his mouth, something about how the country apparently didn't want new voters very badly.

He went upstairs and did what he always did instead of worrying, which was look things up. The Elections Canada page loaded slowly on his phone. He read it twice. Then he read it a third time, because it seemed too easy. He texted Henry, who had also just turned eighteen and had, characteristically, done nothing at all about any of it.

"Not on the list," he typed. "You can still register at your polling place on election day. They take you right there."

Henry replied with a thumbs up and then, thirty seconds later, "what's a polling place." Robert sent him the link and lay back on his bed. The information changed the shape of the next morning entirely. He had been planning to skip first period, vote at the church on Elm before the lineup built, and get to chemistry by ten. Now he would need documents, and time, and the church on Elm might not even be his polling place if he wasn't on the list, though the site said assigned, which suggested the place was still assigned to him, that the system knew where he belonged even when it didn't know he existed.

At breakfast he told his mother what he had found out, laying it out carefully, the way he did in debates: an eligible voter who wasn't on the list could register at the assigned polling place on election day itself. "So I'm going in with my ID and a piece of mail," he said. "And I'll leave early."

"Take the hydro bill," she said. "It has your name on it from the gym membership thing." She was already half out the door herself, voting on her way to work, a ritual she described every election as the least she could do, a phrase Robert had never quite parsed, since it seemed to be both an understatement and a kind of boast.

At the church on Elm there was a line of folding tables and a woman with a clipboard who asked his name and found nothing, then said, "First time?" in a tone that suggested he was not the first first-time that morning. He showed his driver's licence and the hydro bill. She wrote something, another woman stamped something, and a man in a lanyard walked him to a second table, where a ballot was handed over with the small ceremonial gravity of a key. The whole thing took eleven minutes. He had budgeted forty.

Behind the cardboard screen he read the names. He had read the platforms too, over the past month, partly for a civics assignment and partly because Ariel had argued with him about one of them for an entire lunch period, and he had ended up somewhere between his father's preference and Ariel's, agreeing with the second on the money and the first on the timeline, a position that satisfied no one, including himself.
