He thought briefly of Mr. Smith, who taught chemistry and liked to say that a conclusion you could not test was an opinion, and Robert understood that his ballot was exactly that, an opinion, made as carefully as he could make it.

He marked it, folded it, and fed it into the box. The man with the lanyard said "next" over his shoulder, already looking past him.

Outside he called Ariel. "I did it," he said. "Want to get coffee before school? I'll tell you who I voted for if you promise to yell at me quietly."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Between large parallel plates the field is nearly uniform, so away from the edges a point near one plate has the same field strength as a point midway between them.
story:
The gym smelled of floor wax and hot extension cords, and Seth had spent the first hour of the science fair worrying that his exhibit looked smaller than everyone else's. Around him, volcano models fizzed and a robot arm knocked over a tower of blocks on schedule. His own table held two aluminum plates mounted on a wooden frame, a battery pack, and a hand-lettered sign: THE FIELD BETWEEN THE PLATES. He had a voltmeter, a ruler, and a plan that had seemed airtight at his kitchen table the night before.

The plan was to measure the electric field strength at points between the plates and show how it changed. He had imagined a graph, a curve, something a judge could look at and see at once that he understood what he was doing. He had even prepared a table with columns for the distance to the bottom plate and the distance to the top plate, because obviously both would matter.

"You're measuring again," Frederic said. Frederic's table was two rows over, a display about water filtration, but he kept drifting back to watch. Frederic wanted the regional slot, the one the fair sent only one project to, and he had said so in the parking lot without apology. "Third time."

"I want it exact," Seth said. He crouched with the ruler, marking a point a centimeter above the bottom plate, then another a centimeter below the top one. "Near the bottom plate the field should be stronger. It's closer to the charge. So I need the distance to each plate for every measurement." It sounded right when he said it. It had sounded right for forty minutes.

Frederic leaned against the table edge, arms folded, not quite hiding that he was pleased. "You're going to run out of time before you run out of points."

Mr. Janssen came by before lunch. He was the physics teacher from the other high school, the one brought in to judge the senior division, and he moved down the aisle with a clipboard and a circumspect expression, giving each project the same unhurried look. At Seth's table he stopped, read the sign, and picked up the voltmeter probe without asking.

"What are you finding?" he said.

Seth showed him the table, the columns, the two distances. "I'm mapping how the field changes with position," he said. "I've done four points so far. Near the bottom plate, near the top, and two in between." He hesitated, because here was the part he did not want to say out loud. "The numbers all came out the same. I thought I was doing something wrong."

Mr. Janssen set the probe down. He looked at the table for a long moment, and Seth had a presentiment, sudden and specific, that he had made a fool of himself in front of the one person here who would know.

"Do it again," Mr. Janssen said. "Right there, midway. Then move it wherever you like, away from the edges. Tell me what you see." And he stepped back, giving Seth nothing else, already glancing toward Frederic's filtration display as though the conversation were over.

Seth worked. He put the probe midway between the plates and read the meter. He moved it closer to the bottom plate, well away from the sides of the frame, and read again. He moved it near the top plate. Each time the needle settled in the same place, and each time he wrote the number down and stared at it as though it might change under scrutiny. He stopped measuring the distances. There was nothing to measure them for. Between large parallel plates like his, the field was nearly uniform, and he had spent an hour behaving as though each point needed its own arithmetic, as though the middle were special. A point near one plate had the same field strength as a point midway between them. He had gotten it wrong in the planning and found it out in the doing, which was, he admitted to himself, probably how most things got found out.

He redrew the graph. Not a curve: a flat line, steady all the way across, with the measurements scattered just above and below it like quiet evidence. He wrote a new caption under it, then crossed out the word "wrong" and wrote "uniform" instead, and under that, small, "except near the edges, where I couldn't measure."

Frederic appeared again with ten minutes left before judging, hands in his pockets. He looked at the flat line for a while. "So the whole distance thing," he said. "You didn't need it."

"No," Seth said. "I needed it. I just needed it to be wrong first."

Frederic frowned at that, then laughed, a short, unwilling sound. "Janssen looked at my filters for about a minute," he said. "He looked at your line for three." He said it lightly, but he was looking at the graph the whole time, and his jaw was tight.

When the judges gathered at the front of the gym, clipboard in hand, Mr. Janssen paused beside Seth's table on his way past. He tapped the caption, the word "uniform," with one finger.

"Say that part again," he said. "The part you wrote small."

"Except near the edges," Seth said. "Where I couldn't measure."

Mr. Janssen wrote something on the clipboard, unreadable, and moved on toward the front of the gym, where the microphone was being switched on.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook.
story:
The pasta was supposed to have been done eight minutes ago. Laurie lifted a strand from the pot, blew on it, and bit down; the outside had gone soft but the center snapped like a pencil lead. Behind her, on the card table her father had dragged out from the garage, the rest of the dinner waited in stages: sauce warming in a dented saucepan, a bowl of salad going warm too, because the backyard was the only place her mother's kitchen remodel left them to cook.

"Twenty minutes," her father called from the door, holding his phone up like a stopwatch. "Your mother's flight lands in twenty and the car needs to pick her up. If we're not eating when she walks in, she'll say it's fine, and it will not be fine."

Laurie had done everything right, or everything she knew how to do. Eleven minutes, the box said, and she had given it eleven, then three more, then a fourth while telling herself the timer on her phone was wrong. She stirred the pot again and the shells turned over slowly, pale and stubborn, and she felt the specific humiliation of a person who has followed instructions and been betrayed by them.

She texted Addison, who had spent the summer at her uncle's place in the mountains and would know, or would pretend to. Pasta still hard after way past the box time, Laurie typed. Am I losing my mind. The answer came back in under a minute, which meant Addison had been waiting for something to do. You're not losing your mind. Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, like 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet. So boiled food takes longer to cook. Add time. That's why everything at my uncle's took forever.

Laurie looked up from the phone, over the fence, at the scrubby hill behind the neighbors' roofline, at the whole town sitting up here where she had lived for eighteen years without once thinking about the boiling point of her own stove. It was not a betrayal, then. It was a fact she had never needed until tonight. "It's the altitude," she said out loud, to no one, and then, louder, to her father: "The water boils cooler up here. Everything takes longer."

"So how much longer?"

"I don't know yet." She said it without apology, which was new for her. She fished out another shell, tested it, added four minutes to the timer and watched the pot as if her attention could be an ingredient. The sauce was beginning to catch on the bottom of the pan, so she moved it off the direct flame and stirred in a splash of water to resuscitate it, working the sticky edges back into something smooth. It wasn't ruined. It was nearly ruined, which was a different thing.

Her father came out with two folding chairs and set them at the card table with a nonchalant air that did not fool her. He wanted to seem like a man untroubled by schedules, standing in his own backyard with his phone counting down in his pocket. "Your grandmother used to say this town was too high for proper cooking," he said. "I thought she was complaining about the oven."

"She was complaining about the water, apparently."

"Same thing, at her altitude."

Laurie laughed, and then the timer went off and she was testing shells again, one after another, discarding the failures into the saucepan where they could at least hide. On the fourth test the pasta gave all the way through, no chalky line in the center, and she drained the pot with the colander braced against the table's edge while steam rose into the dusk and the cicadas in the hedge started up like a crowd settling.

The table came together fast after that: pasta into a bowl, sauce over it, salad that had wilted but would be eaten anyway. Her father counted out bread from the bag with the gravity of a man making a final disbursement from a dwindling treasury, three slices for her, two for himself, the rest held in reserve for her mother. He had just set the last fork down when headlights swept the fence.

"See," he said, straightening the bowl so the chipped side faced away from the door. "Fine."

"That's not fine," Laurie said. "That's on time."

The gate latch clicked, and her mother came through it with her suitcase still in hand, stopping at the edge of the lawn to look at the steaming bowl, the lit citronella candle, the two chairs and the one her father was dragging over for her. "You cooked," she said.

"We cooked," Laurie said, and lifted the serving spoon. "Sit down before it gets cold. Up here, everything takes longer, so we made sure it wouldn't have to."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food-safety guidance says refrigerated food must be kept at or below 4 degrees Celsius (40 degrees Fahrenheit) to slow the growth of bacteria.
story:
Maria had signed up for the community garden shift because her mother had proselytized about it all through dinner, twice, and it was easier to agree than to keep chewing in silence. Now she stood at the garden's edge on a Saturday morning, holding a clipboard she had been handed by a woman in a sun hat, wondering what exactly she had agreed to. The garden shared a chain-link fence with the food bank, and the two operations seemed to run into each other like tides, wheelbarrows going one way, boxes of donated groceries going the other.

"You're the new one," said a girl in canvas gloves, appearing beside her with the suddenness of someone who had been waiting behind a trellis. "Jasmin. You look like you're guarding the clipboard. It's not that important."

"I'm Maria. I was told to count something, but she didn't say what."

Jasmin laughed. "Classic Ms. Yoon. She gives everyone a clipboard and lets us figure out the rest. It's her whole philosophy. She'd call it leadership. I'd call it vacation from deciding." She pointed at the low building beyond the fence. "Today the garden crew helps the food bank, because Saturday is delivery day and they're short-handed. Come on, the truck's here."

The loading dock behind the food bank smelled of cardboard and cold dust. Volunteers moved crates of canned beans, sacks of rice, boxes of dented but dignified soup. A man with a hand truck backed through the door, and Ms. Yoon directed traffic with the serene authority of an air traffic controller who had chosen vegetables instead. Maria was handed a box of oranges and told to stack them by weight, which she did, and for ten minutes the work was simple and pleasant, the kind of work that let her mind wander.

Then she nearly tripped over the milk. Four plastic jugs sat in a cluster near the dock's edge, sweating in the sun, well away from the open cooler door. She picked one up and it was faintly warm on one side, like a cat that had been sleeping in a window. "Hey," she said, to nobody in particular. "Hey, Jasmin. Whose milk is this?"

Jasmin came over, looked, and pulled a face. "The driver leaves it there sometimes. He says he'll only be a minute, and then he's not a minute. Why, is it bad?"

"I don't know. Is it?" Maria turned the jug over. The expiration date was two weeks away. "It smells fine. But it's warm."

Judith, a taller girl from Maria's chemistry class whom she knew mostly as the person who borrowed pencils and never returned them, wandered over eating an apple. "There's a thermometer in the cooler," she said. "They check it. My aunt does food safety for a hospital and she goes on about it. Refrigerated food has to stay at or below four degrees Celsius. Forty Fahrenheit, if you like that better."

"That's specific," Maria said.

"That's bacteria," Judith said, with her mouth full. "They like it warm. Well, my aunt likes saying they like it warm. I don't actually know what they like." She shrugged and went back to her apples and her crate of pasta.

Maria stood holding the jug, and two thoughts arrived at the same time and immediately began to argue. The first was her mother's voice, or something like it: waste is a sin, milk costs money, people at a food bank need that milk, and throwing out four jugs over a little sunshine would be exactly the kind of precious fastidiousness that let privilege pretend it was conscience. The second was Judith's aunt, invisible and probably right: warm milk was a gamble with someone else's stomach, someone who had not been offered the chance to decline the gamble. She could not fully believe both. She was not sure she could fully believe either.

"Ms. Yoon," she called, and when the sun hat turned, she held up the jug. "The milk was sitting out on the dock. It's warm on one side. Judith says it has to be at or below four degrees Celsius to be safe. Do we have a thermometer we can stick in it?"

Ms. Yoon crossed the dock, took the jug, pressed it to her cheek like a grandmother testing a fever, and then, decisive, went and got the thermometer from the cooler. They pushed it into the top jug. The numbers climbed and settled. Eight degrees. Jasmin peered over Maria's shoulder and said, "Eight. That's a failing grade in every class I take."

"So it's out," Ms. Yoon said. "All four." She said it simply, without ceremony, and Maria felt a strange small relief, as if someone else had carried the argument for her and set it down.

"I hate that," Maria said, helping carry the jugs to the bin. "It's good milk. It just got left in the sun by somebody's minute."

"It did," Ms. Yoon agreed. "And the person who eats it doesn't get to know that. They just get the minute, or they don't." She snapped the lid. "Next Saturday you can be the one standing on the dock when the truck comes. You can hold the driver to his minute. You seem like someone who will."

"She proselytized at me about compost for twenty minutes yesterday," Jasmin said. "The driver doesn't stand a chance."

"That's not what I did," Maria said. "That was information."

"That's what a proselytizer would say." Jasmin dodged the orange Maria threw at her, laughing, and the orange rolled off the dock and came to rest against the fence, absurd and bright, anachronistic among the cabbages, looking for all the world like it had rolled there on purpose.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: Home equity is the home's current value minus what is still owed on the mortgage.
story:
The spare key was where Etienne said it would be, under the ceramic frog by the door, and Maelle let herself into the apartment carrying two grocery bags and a question she had been carrying for most of the week. Rent was due on the first. Her mother had said it at the kitchen table, flat, the way she said things she did not want to argue about, and then she had said the word "deposit" as if Maelle already knew what it meant, which she did not, not exactly, not the way you know a thing when you might have to pay one.

Etienne was in the kitchen slicing a baguette with more concentration than bread required. His grandmother, who owned the apartment and had for thirty years, sat by the window with the crossword, the arboreal street outside throwing leaf shadows across her lap. "She's selling the house," Etienne said, meaning his grandmother's old place across the city, the one nobody had lived in since his grandfather died. "Sit down, you're pacing."

"I'm not pacing." Maelle set the bags down. "I'm thinking." She was doing both, a small circuit between the counter and the table. Amin arrived before she completed it, damp from the rain, shaking his jacket like a dog and asking immediately what was in the bags.

"Etienne's grandmother," Maelle said, "when you sell the house, where does the money go? All of it, I mean. Like, you just get the price?"

The grandmother lowered the crossword. "You get the price, and out of that comes whatever you still owe the bank."

"You owe the bank on a house you've had forever?"

"That house is paid off, thank God. But my neighbor, the one with the hydrangeas, she refinanced twice. When she sells, the bank takes its share first and she gets what's left." The grandmother tapped her pen against the table, twice, thinking. "It's called equity," she said. "Equity is the home's current value minus what is still owed on the mortgage."

Maelle turned that sentence over the way she turned a formula before she trusted it. Current value minus what was still owed. So the neighbor with the hydrangeas sold the same kind of house and walked away with less, not because the house was worth less, but because some of it still belonged to the bank. She said it back slowly, testing, and the grandmother nodded once and went back to eleven across.

"Wait," Amin said, mouth full of baguette. "So how do you owe the bank in the first place? Where'd the money for the house come from?"

"You borrow it," Etienne said. "Nobody has that much money at once. You save a chunk first, a down payment, and the bank gives you the rest, and you pay it back a little every month for decades. My grandmother says it's the only debt she's ever liked." He slid a plate of cheese toward the middle of the table, a diplomat ending an argument before it started.

Maelle sat down at last. Her family rented, and would keep renting, and the deposit her mother kept mentioning was the landlord's version of insurance: money handed over before you even moved in, held hostage against damage, returned only if you left the place immaculate. It was not the same as a down payment, but it rhymed with one, a threshold you paid to be allowed across a threshold. Both were money you had to have all at once, before you could begin. She had assumed, until tonight, that owning and renting were just two different temperaments, some people careful and some people careless, and now she suspected it was more like two different distances from the same door.

"Do you like it?" she asked the grandmother, meaning the owning, the thirty years of monthly payments to the bank, and the grandmother considered the question longer than crossword clues usually got.

"I liked the day it ended," she said. "The payments were duress, no matter how polite the letters were. But I liked knowing each one bought a little more of the place. Rent never buys anything. It just rents again next month." She enunciated the last part carefully, as though Maelle were copying it down, which in a way she was.

Amin asked whether it was smarter, then, mathematically, to buy, and Etienne said it depended on the price of the place and how long you stayed, and the two of them fell into an argument about an uncle of Amin's who had bought and then had to sell in a bad year. Maelle let it run past her. She was still holding the two ideas side by side, the deposit her mother needed by the first and the equity sitting in a paid-off house across the city, and she could not yet see how a family crossed from one to the other, only that some families did and some, politely, month after month, never did.

"Eleven across," the grandmother announced to the room. "Six letters. 'Cleared, as land of trees.'"

"Deforested," Maelle said, and reached for a piece of cheese.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: About 30 million cubic metres of water per second flow through the Florida Straits in the Gulf Stream, a flow oceanographers call 30 sverdrups.
story:
Sophia had promised her mother she would be home by five, which gave her exactly two hours to understand a river she could not see, running through an ocean she had never visited. The science museum's ocean hall smelled faintly of aquarium salt and hand sanitizer, and the current map covered an entire wall, all of the Atlantic drawn in arrows: red ones snaking up the American coast, curling east, and loosening toward Europe like a hand letting go of a rope.

"Thirty," said Benoit, who had come along because his bus pass worked on Saturdays and he had nothing better to do. He was reading a small brass plaque below the map and tapping it twice, as if it might admit to exaggeration. "Thirty million cubic metres per second, through the Florida Straits. That's the Gulf Stream. The flow is thirty sverdrups."

"Sverdrups," Sophia repeated. The word sat in her mouth like a marble.

"Named after an oceanographer," Benoit said. "Apparently if you're an oceanographer, sometimes they name the unit after you."

"Big if," said Edmond, arriving late with two cookies from the cafe, one of which he offered to Sophia as tribute for his lateness, which she accepted as tax. Edmond was, in his own estimation, a connoisseur of maps, though his expertise was limited to the transit map, which he could navigate blind and would defend against all critics. He studied the wall of arrows with the polite, blasé expression of a man being shown someone else's holiday photographs. "Nice lines. Where's the part where I can get a train somewhere?"

Sophia ignored him, which was the correct response to Edmond and he knew it. She stood close to the map and tried to picture thirty million cubic metres. She tried imagining a swimming pool. Then a thousand swimming pools. Then a thousand swimming pools every single second, forever, squeezing between Florida and Cuba like the whole thing had somewhere urgent to be. Her imagination filed a complaint and lay down. "It can't be real," she said. "Nothing moves that much stuff that fast without somebody noticing."

"The ocean is extremely good at not being noticed," Benoit said. "It's basically its whole strategy."

The problem, the actual problem, the one that had brought her here instead of to the cafe with Edmond, was Ms. Papadopoulos. On Thursday, Sophia had given a presentation in geography in which she claimed, with total confidence and zero evidence, that Europe was warm because it was "just naturally like that," a claim so lazy that Ms. Papadopoulos had spent a full minute excoriating it, in front of everyone, in a voice usually reserved for students who forge signatures. Warm air near Ireland, Ms. Papadopoulos had said, warm oranges grown in places that should be Canadian, and Sophia had sat there flushed and furious and, worse, curious. Monday there would be a chance to explain it properly. Sophia intended to be ready, and she intended, this time, to be right.

So she traced the red arrows with her finger, not touching the wall, hovering a centimetre off the glass. Up the coast. Past the Carolinas. Then the turn, the great eastward sweep toward Ireland and Norway. "Okay," she said slowly. "So the warm water goes north and east, and it gives off its heat along the way. To the air. And the air goes over Europe." She turned to the boys. "That's why London isn't Montreal. London and Montreal are roughly the same latitude, but London gets the tail end of this." She flapped a hand at the map like she was petting an enormous invisible animal.

"Comforting," said Edmond, around his cookie. "I've always felt London deserved it."

"Deserved what?"

"Warmth. Bad weather in London is more picturesque. Warm bad weather. It's a whole aesthetic."

Benoit had drifted to a console near the map, a touchscreen where you could slide a little dial and watch the arrows speed up and slow down. He slid it. The Atlantic obligingly whipped itself into a frenzy of red. "What happens if you turn it off?" he asked the room, and then, before anyone could stop him, he slid the dial all the way down.

The arrows faded to grey and thinned to almost nothing. The labels over Europe shifted, and a small note appeared beside Norway: cooler summers. Sophia stared at it. There was something in the grey map that she couldn't shake, the shape of a Europe she preferred not to think about, and she was honest enough with herself to admit she didn't know if the dial was showing real science or a museum's idea of a warning. "Turn it back," she said.

Benoit turned it back. The red river reassembled itself, thirty million cubic metres per second resuming as though it had never stopped, which, Sophia supposed, was the point of it. It didn't stop. It had been running since long before anyone drew arrows over it, and it would keep running whether or not a girl with a Monday deadline understood it.

She copied the numbers into her notebook: the flow, the straits, the strange word for the unit. She underlined "sverdrups" twice and wrote beside it, in small letters, "ask how you even measure that," because the measuring was the part that still felt impossible, the part where some person, some Dr. Sverdrup or his heirs, stood beside a strait and counted water no one could hold.

"What's Monday's presentation on, again?" Edmond asked, leaning over her notebook and immediately reading things he hadn't been invited to read.

"Why northern Europe is warm."

"Tell them it's the arrows," Edmond said, pointing at the wall with the last of his cookie. "People love arrows."

Sophia closed her notebook and looked up at the great red sweep of it, still curling east, still letting go of the coast. "Tell you what," she said. "Monday, you're the map."

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Socialist politician Jean Jaurès wrote a socialist history of the French Revolution in the early 1900s that shaped the class-conflict interpretation dominant for much of the twentieth century.
story:
Olivia would like it recorded, first of all, that she had not left the essay until the last minute. She had left it until the second-to-last minute, which was a completely different thing, and she had the color-coded plan to prove it, folded into her back pocket like a treaty nobody intended to honor. The public library on Delmore Street had the advantage of being open until nine, the further advantage of a third-floor history section nobody visited except a man who appeared to be asleep near the atlases, and the decisive advantage of being where Kaydence had agreed to meet her at seven with snacks and what Kaydence called moral infrastructure.

The assignment sheet, crumpled but legible, asked for a historiographical essay: not what happened in the French Revolution, but how views of it had changed since 1800. "Two thousand words on why historians can't agree," Mr. Whitehead had said in class, in the tone of a man handing out fireworks. Olivia had nodded along, feeling scholarly, and had then spent a week reading about Marie Antoinette's hair, which was not on the syllabus but was extremely interesting.

At the table by the window, Kaydence slid a paper bag across and pulled out her phone. "Okay, so my cousin did this memorial thing in France last summer," she said. "Some town square, wall with names from old wars. She took pictures because she photographs everything, including, like, parking garages." She turned the screen. There was a stone wall, weathered, a list of names, and near the bottom, circled in the photo app's red ink, JAURÈS. "She says he was assassinated in 1914. That's all she knows. She kept saying it like it was a crossword clue."

"Jean Jaurès," Olivia read off the plaque below the name in the photo, "député." She typed the name into the library catalogue, mostly to prove to herself that she was working, and felt an actual physical jolt when the screen offered more than she expected. Not a soldier's biography. Books. A multivolume history. "Kaydence. He was a historian. A socialist politician who wrote a socialist history of the French Revolution in the early nineteen hundreds."

"Your fun is so weird," Kaydence said, unwrapping a muffin.

The third floor smelled like carpet and patience. Olivia found the volumes shelved between heavier, duller neighbors and carried three of them down in a stack that obliged her to walk slowly, like a small ceremonial procession. In the margin of her notebook, in Rami's handwriting, there was a note he had slipped her after class two days ago, which she had told herself she'd already considered and privately believed she had: "Olivia, you keep asking what the Revolution meant. Wrong question, obviously. Ask what each century needed it to mean. Historians are not judges, they are mirrors with footnotes. P.S. Your plan is a decoration, not a plan. Start writing." She had described this note to Kaydence as "bickering," which was generous; it had been a small, accurate ambush.

She read. Jaurès had seen the Revolution as a story of classes in conflict, which sounded obvious until Olivia realized it had not been obvious to anyone before him, and then it had been obvious to nearly everyone for decades afterward. Textbooks after Jaurès explained the Revolution his way, the class-conflict way, through what the introduction called much of the twentieth century, until historians began pulling the interpretation apart again, asking about culture and politics and contingency, the way you re-question a witness who has been believed too long. The scale of it exhilarated her: one argument, made by one man in the early 1900s, bending a hundred years of classrooms. Her own draft, she now saw, had simply inherited the bend and called it common sense. That stung, briefly, and then it didn't, because it was also the essay. The essay was this. The disagreement was the subject.

Mr. Whitehead appeared at the end of the aisle at eight-thirty, holding a book he clearly had no intention of checking out, the way librarians' most persistent patrons do. "Finding it tenable up here?" he asked. "That's a genuine question, not a pun. Most students find the third floor spiritually inhospitable."

"It's fine," Olivia said. "I found the guy from the memorial."

"The guy from the memorial," Mr. Whitehead repeated, delighted, and put the book back on the wrong shelf while pretending to straighten it.

At the table she spread her notes into the shape of an argument, or at least the shape of an argument's skeleton awaiting a verdict. Jaurès on one side, the revisionists on the other, and herself in the middle, writing a sentence she liked and then distrusting it and then liking it again. It was not tenable to claim any single interpretation had won, so she would claim something smaller and harder: that each version of the Revolution told the truth about the people writing it, and that a reader who knew that could read everything twice. Whether that was insight or a dodge she genuinely did not know, and she wrote that uncertainty into the conclusion, feeling both fraudulent and pleased.

Kaydence read the last paragraph over her shoulder, chewing. "So your answer is, everyone's right a little and wrong a little?"

"Everyone's right a lot and wrong a lot, actually," Olivia said, and then, in a spirit of disclosure, "also Rami wrote half of my second paragraph by yelling at me on Tuesday."

Kaydence looked up from the phone, grinning. "You told me you hadn't even read his note."

The library lights clicked, the nine o'clock warning, and Olivia began stacking the volumes, the Jaurès on top, its cloth cover soft as an old coat. "Check the memorial wall again," she said. "Check who circled the name and why." Kaydence scrolled, and scrolled, and then held up the phone: beneath the photo, in her cousin's caption, a line Olivia had not been shown, dated last summer, before the assignment even existed. "Mr. Whitehead was on this trip too. He's the one who said to look this guy up."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: If the forward reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants, because the system absorbs the added heat by running in reverse.
story:
Maelie set the two sealed tubes on the kitchen table beside the electric kettle, then moved them again, farther from the steam, as though their contents might already be listening. The tubes had come from Ms. Zhou, the retired teacher two doors down who kept a cabinet of old lab supplies and lent them out with the air of a woman releasing prisoners on parole. Inside each tube was a gas that shifted between pale and brown depending, the handwritten card said, on conditions. For the regional science fair, Maelie had built her whole poster around predicting which way it would go. Heat it, she had written in her proposal, and it darkens, because heat drives the forward reaction forward.

Alex arrived at four with a bag of chips and the querulous announcement that the bus had been twenty minutes late, which in Alex's view was part of a wider collapse of public infrastructure and possibly of the national character. Maelie had texted a single line that morning: it has to be today. The fair was Saturday. She had collated her data from three practice runs, printed the graphs, mounted them on foam board, and everything depended on the demonstration working the way her poster claimed it would.

"Explain it to me again," Alex said, sitting on the counter with the chips balanced on one knee. "Like I'm a person who took biology on purpose."

"There's an equilibrium," Maelie said. "The reaction goes both ways at once, and the mixture settles at a balance point. Le Chatelier said if you disturb it, the system shifts to counteract the disturbance." She plugged in the kettle. "So if you add heat, the system should shift to soak up the heat. My reaction, the forward one, is written right here as the one that takes heat in. Add heat, forward reaction runs, more of the brown gas. Darker tube." She tapped the foam board where the arrow was, where she had copied it weeks ago from a worksheet and never looked at it again.

She held the first tube over the kettle's spout with tongs, at arm's length, the way Ms. Zhou had demonstrated with exaggerated caution. Steam curled around the glass. The gas inside was pale, almost colorless, with the faintest tea-colored tinge at the bottom. The thermometer clipped to the stand read the room temperature of the kitchen, and Maelie noted it on her clipboard, her handwriting smaller than usual.

The color began to change. Alex leaned in off the counter, and neither of them spoke, and the kettle kept breathing, and for a long moment the only sound was the low rumble of the element. The brown deepened, and deepened, and then, as the tube passed a certain warmth under Maelie's careful hand, it did the one thing she had not planned for. It began to fade. The color drained upward from the bottom like sediment settling in reverse, until the tube hung pale and empty-looking in the steam, paler than it had started, while her poster behind her, in confident black marker, promised darker.

"That's backwards," Alex said.

"I know it's backwards."

"Is it the tube? Maybe Ms. Zhou's tubes are old."

Maelie set the tongs down. She went back through her notebook, page by page, the practice runs, the proposal, and finally the photocopy of the original worksheet, and there it was, the thing she had been reading past all along. The thermochemical equation carried its little symbol beside the products, the mark she had assumed belonged to the reverse direction because she had never actually checked. The forward reaction was exothermic. It gave heat out. Which meant that when she added heat, the system countered her by running backward, absorbing what she had put in, consuming the brown gas and leaving her with exactly the pale tube she was holding. Everything she had written about which way it shifted was true, and it shifted against her.

She thought of arguing with the tube, briefly, the way she had argued with a substitute teacher in tenth grade who turned out to be right. Instead she sat down across from the foam board and looked at it honestly, her prediction and her result side by side, two accounts of the same event that could not both stand. The zeitgeist of every science fair she had ever visited came back to her: boards that only ever confirmed themselves, hypotheses that won every time, and she had nearly joined them by deleting the afternoon and reprinting the poster with the wrong arrows flipped quietly in the dark.

Ms. Zhou answered her door in a cardigan with tea in one hand, and listened to the whole confession without a change of expression. "The sealed tubes aren't old," she said. "But you can't know that from one afternoon."

"That's the part I hate," Maelie said. "I have one clean run and one failed prediction, and I can't tell from the inside whether I understand it or whether I just want to."

Ms. Zhou drank her tea. "Then show the failed one."

Maelie walked home in the blue evening, carrying the tubes in a padded lunch bag against her chest. In the kitchen, Alex had laid out the second tube, the cold water bath, and a fresh sheet of poster paper with the heading half-lettered in pencil: what I predicted, what happened. She picked up the pencil, and beside her first claim wrote the second, both of them visible now, neither erased.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: In a definite integral the constant of integration cancels out, because it is added to both F(b) and F(a) and then subtracted away.
story:
Blake kept the test folded in his back pocket all through Thursday, and when he finally spread it across the table at the tutoring centre, the red mark at the corner of page two had gone soft from handling. Minus four. The same integral he had checked three times, the one where he had found the antiderivative and evaluated at the upper limit, evaluated at the lower limit, subtracted, and then, out of caution, added plus C. The marker's pen had circled the C like a wound.

"It's right, though," he said. "The number's right."

Lilly leaned over from the next table, where she was supposed to be transcribing her chemistry notes onto index cards but was mostly drawing arrows between them. "It's a definite integral," she said. "You gave them the area. The whole thing."

"That's what I don't get. More information is more right. Isn't it?"

Beckham, who had come for calculus help and stayed for the free coffee, pulled the paper toward him as if the answer might be legible from a different angle. "My cousin says plus C is for the other kind. The indefinite ones." He said this with the confidence of a man reporting weather from a city he had never visited.

Mr. Levy, who ran the centre and drifted between tables with a mug that never seemed to empty, paused long enough to read the problem, then kept walking. "You already have everything you need," he said over his shoulder, which Blake found genuinely unhelpful, though later he would decide it was the kindest thing anyone had said to him all week.

He stayed after Beckham left for practice. Lilly stayed too, pretending her flashcards weren't finished. Blake took a fresh sheet and wrote the antiderivative twice, once for the upper limit and once for the lower, and then, underneath, the subtraction, the long horizontal bar with F of b above and F of a below. He wrote C after each one, because that was the habit, the reflex drilled in over weeks of indefinite integrals where forgetting it cost you marks. Then he sat back and looked at what he had written.

"Oh," he said.

"What?"

"Look at it. I add C when I plug in the top. I add C when I plug in the bottom." His pencil tapped the fraction bar. "Then I subtract. It cancels. It's in both, so it goes away." He crossed out the two C's with a single stroke each, feeling something click into place that felt less like learning a rule and more like being shown a door he had been pushing on its hinge side. The area was just the difference. The constant never had a chance to matter.

Lilly frowned at the sheet. "So it was there and then it wasn't."

"It was never really there. I put it there. That's why the four marks, I guess. I gave an answer to a question nobody asked." He copied the corrected version onto the test margin, not because anyone would regrade it, but so the paper would stop bothering him. Still, something about it nagged at him, the way the C sat on both lines, identical, patient, subtracting itself out of existence. He couldn't decide whether that was reassuring or a little lonely, and he said so, and Lilly said that was the most Beckham thing he had ever said, which he chose to take as a compliment.

Mr. Levy stopped at their table on his way to lock the storeroom and looked at the crossed-out C's for a long moment. "You'll forget this by Monday," he said, but he was almost smiling.

Blake didn't forget it. That was the problem. On Monday's quiz, question four asked for the indefinite integral of the same function, a general antiderivative, no limits anywhere, and Blake moved through it cleanly, confident, unhurried, and at the very end, out of a new and hard-won suspicion of constants, he left the C off entirely.

When the papers came back on Wednesday, there was a red circle where the plus C should have been, and Lilly leaned across the aisle and whispered, "More information is more right. Isn't it?"

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: In the tabling method, melted chocolate is spread and worked on a cool marble slab to bring its temperature down and start stable crystals forming.
story:
Eve had promised herself she would learn to temper chocolate before she left for college, and she had exactly one afternoon left at Jonah's house to do it, because his kitchen had the one thing hers did not: a slab of cool marble the size of a door laid into the counter, left over from when his mother still baked.

"Leighton says you don't need the marble," Jonah said, setting two bars of dark chocolate on the counter and unwrapping one with the care of someone defusing something. "He says you just melt it and put it in the fridge and it sets fine."

"Then it's gray and it bends." Eve had read the same three paragraphs of the same book so many times she could almost recite them, and the word she kept circling was "tabling." The method was called tabling, and it involved spreading the melted chocolate out on the cool marble and working it back and forth with a spatula until the temperature came down. That was the part she understood. The part she only half understood was what the marble was starting, the crystals, the stable ones, forming somewhere in the liquid where she couldn't see them.

Leighton arrived while the chocolate was still in the bowl over the pan of barely simmering water, carrying a thermometer he'd borrowed from the chemistry lab like it was contraband. "I contextualized it for you," he announced. "Chocolate, crystals, phase transitions. It's basically applied chemistry, which means I'm basically indispensable."

"You're basically holding a thermometer," Jonah said.

The chocolate reached temperature and Eve poured perhaps a third of it onto the marble, where it spread in a dark ribbon and immediately began to lose its gloss at the edges. Then came the part the book could not prepare her for. She dragged the spatula through it, gathered it, spread it thin again, and the chocolate resisted, thickened, caught under the blade. Her wrist ached within two minutes. The motion was less like stirring than like plastering, like convincing something stubborn to become briefly something else.

"You're losing it," Leighton said, leaning over her shoulder with the thermometer. "It's going too fast."

"It's supposed to go fast." She wasn't sure that was true. She only knew that somewhere in the smear on the marble, the temperature was coming down, and the stable crystals were forming, and she couldn't see them, couldn't feel them, could only trust that the working was doing what working was supposed to do. It occurred to her, in the middle of a stroke, that this was the opposite of how she'd been taught everything for twelve years. At school, understanding came first and then you did the thing. Here the doing came first and the understanding, if it came at all, would have to be inferred afterward, from a shine she wouldn't see until the chocolate had set.

She scraped the thickened chocolate back into the bowl with the warmer remainder, stirred, and dipped the edge of a knife. The chocolate on the blade dried in what felt like no time at all, and when she touched it, it was smooth and dry, no bloom, no tackiness. She broke off a flake and it snapped, a small clean sound like a knuckle cracking, and Leighton said "huh" in a tone she decided to accept as tribute.

Jonah's want revealed itself only then. He had been quiet through most of it, fetching the bowl, wiping the marble, and when Eve offered him the knife he held the shard of chocolate up to the window and looked through it rather than eating it. "My mom used to do this," he said. "At Christmas. She'd do the whole thing, the spreading, the snapping, the little paper cups. I thought if you learned it, I could watch it again." He turned the shard so the light moved across its surface. "That sounds like an affectation when I say it out loud."

"It sounds like you miss her," Eve said, and he put the shard in his mouth instead of answering.

They dipped the last of the chocolate onto parchment in messy coins and Leighton, who had abandoned all pretense of scientific detachment, drew a tiny seismograph line through one of them and called the result tectonic. Eve laughed even though it wasn't quite a joke. When she peeled her first coin off the paper an hour later, it shone like something lacquered, and she snapped it in half, and the halves gleamed clean at the break, and she held one half out to Jonah across the marble slab still streaked pale with what was left of the working.

"Your turn," she said.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The Stanley Cup, donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston and first awarded in 1893, is the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America.
story:
The community field had two games that Saturday, and only one of them mattered to most of the crowd. Paige stood at the chain-link fence with her jacket zipped to her chin, watching her little brother's soccer final stumble toward a nil-nil draw while behind her, on the big screen the rec department had wheeled out under the pavilion, the third period of the Cup final was about to start. Her grandmother had run the field's trophy case for thirty-one years, and now the pavilion was scheduled for demolition on Monday, case and all.

Ms. Rao had the injunction paperwork folded in her back pocket, though she kept saying it was a long shot. "It stops the bulldozers for ninety days," she told Paige that morning, tapping the paper against the fence. "It doesn't stop them forever. A judge doesn't care about feelings, only about whether the county followed its own rules." Paige had spent the week feeling like the case was something she ought to defend without being able to say why, and the ninety days felt like a countdown she had personally failed to extend.

Payten arrived at halftime with a folding table and a cash box, because Payten's family ran a sports memorabilia business and had a plan. "We raffle the old trophies," she said, spreading a sheet of numbered tickets across the table. "People pay twenty bucks a ticket, we make enough to fund the new pavilion, everybody wins. The trophies are just sitting in a case. Sitting there, they're worth nothing. We commodify them and they save the field." She said it the way she said everything, like the logic was already finished and the rest of the world was catching up.

"They're not nothing," Paige said. "That's the whole point of them."

"They're metal cups, Paige. Some of them don't even have names on them anymore."

The screen behind them cut to the Cup itself, bright and enormous, being carried along the boards, and the crowd noise from the pavilion swelled so loudly that a few of the soccer parents turned around. Paige had looked it up on Tuesday night, after the demolition notice went up, because she wanted ammunition and hadn't known where else to find it. The Stanley Cup, donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston and first awarded in 1893, was the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America. She had read the sentence four times. Something that old was still being fought over, still being lifted over grown men's heads while they wept into their beards.

She tried it out now, standing at Payten's table with her hands in her pockets. "You know the Cup is the oldest trophy still awarded to a pro team in North America? Donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston, first awarded in 1893. A hundred and whatever years, and they don't raffle it off to fund a parking lot."

"The Cup is worth millions," Payten said. "Our trophies are worth scrap."

"That's not why it matters. If it mattered because of money, the money would be the thing, and you could just sell the story of it, or the shape of it, and melt the original down."

Payten looked at her for a second, and something in her face shifted, the way it did when a price came in lower than she'd expected and she had to decide whether to say so. "My dad melted down a case like this once," she said. "In Brampton. Bought the trophies for forty dollars each and scrapped the silver." She began stacking the raffle tickets back into the box, unhurried, not quite looking at Paige. "Nobody came to the sale except me."

The final ended on a goal with forty seconds left, and the pavilion crowd screamed and hugged and somebody's little sister cried for no reason she could name. Ms. Rao came over with the injunction paperwork still in her pocket and asked, quietly, whether Paige actually wanted the trophies moved somewhere safe tonight, since the case was coming out either way, injunction or not. Paige said yes before she had finished deciding. It took three of them an hour, kneeling on the cold concrete with bubble wrap, and the case, emptied, looked destitute under the floodlights, its shelves stained in pale rectangles where the cups had stood.

At the bottom shelf, wrapped last, was the oldest one, the founding trophy from 1963, and when Paige turned it over to tape the bubble wrap, she found a small engraving she had never noticed, running along the base in letters gone shallow with polishing. Payten leaned in over her shoulder, read it, and started to laugh, and then stopped herself, and then said it anyway. "It says 'second place, county invitational.' It's not even ours." Paige held the trophy in both hands, the floodlights buzzing, the crowd gone, and read the line again. "Well," she said. "Then we've been guarding the wrong cup for fifty years. Bring the box."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In a 2011 Stanford study, basketball players who aimed for 10 hours in bed nightly improved their free-throw average from 7.9 to 8.8 successful shots out of 10.
story:
The gym smelled of floor wax and cold rubber, and Riley spread his notebook on the bleachers like a surveyor laying out a claim. Monday, lateral drills. Tuesday, shooting until his palm printed the ball's seams into his skin. Wednesday, sprints. Thursday, more shooting. Friday, scrimmage. He wrote Saturday and Sunday, then crossed them out, then wrote them back in lighter pencil, as if the graphite itself were negotiating. Mr. Gallagher had assigned the program three weeks ago and would collect it Friday, and Riley intended to hand over something that looked like ambition.

"You've got no rest days," Sacha said, dropping onto the bench beside him with a water bottle that leaked a slow ring onto the page. Sacha played point guard and read people the way Riley read play diagrams, which was to say too well.

"Rest is for people who are behind."

"Rest is for people who want to get ahead." Sacha tapped the notebook. "Ask Gallagher. He failed a kid last year for a program with no warm-ups."

Riley had a warm-up, technically. It said, in small letters at the top of Monday: jog. It did not say how far, or how fast, or what came after, and they both knew it was a signature on a blank page. He closed the notebook. He would fix it at home, where the planning happened anyway, in the hours after midnight when the house went quiet and he could hear himself think, or something he had decided to call thinking.

That night he sat at his desk at one in the morning revising the grid. Warm-up: dynamic stretching, ten minutes, ankle mobility. Cool-down: same. He underlined the words, and the underlining seemed to underwrite the whole plan, to certify that his body would survive what his ambition had drafted. At two he was still there, adding a Thursday shooting progression, five spots, ten shots each, percentages to be logged. At 2:40 his mother's door stayed dark down the hall and the steppe of the empty kitchen stretched between them, silent and treeless, and he went to bed without noticing he had crossed it.

The next afternoon the gym had been divided into stations, and Mr. Gallagher called it application day. Free throws, ten each, a partner charting. Riley went first because Sacha refused to, standing at the line with the ball squared and his legs loose from the jog he'd actually done, for once. He made seven. Then nine the second set. Then, in the third, six, his elbow drifting, the rim rejecting the ball with a flat clang that echoed off the vaulted ceiling. He shot the seventh short, the eighth long, and stood there breathing through his nose.

"You're getting worse as we go," Sacha said, not unkindly, marking the page. "That's backwards."

"It's one bad set."

"You've been like this all week. Monday you fell asleep in Gallagher's class with your eyes open. I watched you."

Riley wiped his face with the hem of his shirt. Under the high windows the light was already thickening toward evening, his whole diurnal rhythm slipped sideways, and he knew it, had known it for days the way you know a door is unlocked in a house you've already left. He told Sacha about the notebook, the hours, the program that was perfect on paper and had started eating him off it.

Sacha didn't say what he'd expected, which was sleep more, obviously. Instead Sacha pulled out a phone, scrolled, and turned the screen toward him. It was a screenshot of a study, Stanford, 2011. "Read the numbers," Sacha said, and Riley read them slowly, the gym noise receding around the small lit rectangle. Basketball players who aimed for ten hours in bed nightly improved their free-throw average from 7.9 to 8.8 successful shots out of 10. Not practiced more. Slept more. He read it twice, and the second time he heard his own voice in his head arguing against it, all his midnight certainty about reps and grids, and the argument was smaller than he'd remembered.

"That's almost a full shot," Riley said. "Out of ten. From sleeping."

"From aiming for ten hours in bed."

Mr. Gallagher's whistle cut across the stations and they rotated, Riley moving to the corner spot with the chart and Sacha to the line. Sacha made eight, then eight, then nine, smooth as poured water, and Riley watched him and understood that the program he'd built was a plan for a body he was pretending to have, a machine that never needed repair, while the actual machine standing at the desk at two in the morning was running its own schedule and had opinions.

That night he rewrote the grid in pen. Monday, drills, lights out by ten. Tuesday, shooting, sleep. Wednesday, sprints, then rest, a whole word alone in a box, not crossed out. Thursday he left half-blank on purpose, and it looked, to his surprise, like confidence rather than laziness. He set the alarm for ten and turned off the lamp, and across the hall his mother's door opened, footsteps crossing the kitchen steppe toward water, and he lay listening to the ordinary sounds of the house until they, and he, went quiet.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Researcher Amy Edmondson described 'psychological safety' in 1999 as a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake.
story:
The party was Elianna's, in a backyard where her father had built a fire pit that was technically illegal under a town ordinance about open flames within fifteen feet of a fence, though nobody had ever reported it. Hailey arrived late, holding a gift bag and rehearsing a sentence she had not yet managed to say out loud.

The sentence concerned Casey. They were both on the robotics team, and four days earlier Casey had run the demonstration for Mr. Van Dijk's class, and the arm had jammed on the third pass because of a line of code everyone had seen in the shared file. Nobody had said anything. Not Elianna, not the other two builders, not Hailey. Casey had stood at the front of the room saying "it usually works" while eleven people watched the arm knock over a cup it was supposed to lift, and every one of them let her keep believing the problem was the motor.

Hailey had gone home that night and typed into the library database: why won't teams point out errors. She had expected something vague, but the first result was a paper from 1999 by a researcher named Amy Edmondson. It described what she called psychological safety, a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake. Hailey read it twice. It named the thing she had done, or failed to do, and it did not let her call it kindness.

At the fire pit now, Elianna was toasting marshmallows for a group that included Casey, who was sitting on an overturned milk crate with her sleeves pushed up, laughing at something Hailey hadn't heard. Hailey's plan had felt altruistic on the walk over, a good deed she was doing for a teammate before the regional competition. Standing here, it felt more like an ordinance she was enforcing on herself, a rule passed by a committee of one.

There was a flashback she kept returning to. Seventh grade, the science fair, her own project. A girl named nothing now, only the tall girl with the clipboard, had told Hailey in front of the whole gym that her graph was mislabeled and her data didn't support her conclusion. Hailey had cried in the bathroom and never thanked her. Two weeks later, at the actual fair, a judge pointed out the same mislabeled graph, and it cost her a placing. The tall girl had been right and had also been cruel, and the two facts had lived side by side in Hailey's memory for four years without her finding a way to reconcile them. That was the problem with Edmondson's idea, or at least with applying it. You could believe the team was safe and still be wrong about what safety required.

She sat down on the grass next to the milk crate. "Can I tell you something about the demo?"

Casey wiped marshmallow off her fingers. "The arm."

"The arm." Hailey kept her voice level. "It's not the motor. Line forty in the lift sequence. The delay is set wrong, so the gripper closes before the arm gets to the cup. We all saw it in the file." She had decided to include herself in the we, partly because it was true and partly because it made the sentence easier to carry.

Casey looked at the fire for a moment. "I figured it out Tuesday night," she said. "I was waiting to see how long it would take anyone to tell me." She pulled her phone from her pocket and turned the screen toward Hailey. The file was open. Line forty was fixed, dated Wednesday. "I wanted to know if we had it," Casey said. "What Mr. Van Dijk put on the whiteboard that day. Psychological safety. A shared belief it's safe to take interpersonal risks, like admitting a mistake. Edmondson, 1999. It's going to be on the quiz."

"So you tested us."

"You passed with a D minus." Casey laughed, and then stopped. "Except Elianna knew too. She told me Thursday she'd noticed it and didn't want to embarrass me."

Hailey looked across the fire at Elianna, who was handing a marshmallow to a boy from their homeroom and had not volunteered any of this. The warmth in Hailey's chest cooled into something more careful. She had spent the walk here believing she was the honest one.

Casey threw a stick into the flames. "So now you have to tell her she was wrong to wait."

Hailey opened her mouth, and found that nothing came out. Casey watched her, waiting, and said, "You can start with 'can I tell you something.'"

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: In the mitochondrial matrix, each pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA, releasing one molecule of carbon dioxide.
story:
The science museum had a room called The Power Plant, which Aiden thought was an unfortunate name until he realized the pun was intentional, because the exhibit was about mitochondria, which the banner over the door claimed were "the power plants of the cell." He stood under the banner with his phone in one hand and a laminated study sheet in the other, waiting for Elisa and Samantha to finish arguing about where to put their coats.

The three of them had a bio test on Monday, and Ms. Nair had offered extra credit to anyone who could stand in front of the respiration exhibit and walk through the whole pathway out loud, from glucose to ATP, without notes. Samantha had claimed the offer immediately. Elisa had demurred, saying she would rather fail than perform biochemistry in public, but she had come anyway, which told Aiden everything about how worried she actually was.

The exhibit was a long hallway lit like the inside of a cell, with oversized models of molecules floating from the ceiling. Glucose hung at the entrance like a chandelier made of licorice. Aiden walked under it, ducking a dangling phosphate group, and started reciting. "Glucose gets split in glycolysis, that happens in the cytoplasm, makes two pyruvates, and then the pyruvates get shipped into the mitochondria."

"Wrong," said Samantha, without looking up from her phone where she was filming him for evidence, in case Ms. Nair did not believe them.

"What is wrong about that? That is literally correct."

"You said mitochondria. Say mitochondrial matrix. Ms. Nair will mark you down for saying mitochondria like the pyruvate just wanders in through the front door."

Aiden conceded the point with a bow, which in the low light made him clip his head on a floating water molecule. Elisa laughed so hard she had to sit down on a bench shaped, for reasons no one could explain, like a giant kidney.

The argument started at the doorway to the matrix section. There was a big sign there about the link reaction, and Samantha stopped in front of it, frowning, and said, "Okay, wait. Here's what I don't get. When does the first carbon dioxide actually show up? Because I said in class it was the Krebs cycle, and Marcus said I was wrong, and Ms. Nair did that face."

"The face," said Elisa, "where she looks like she's buffering."

"Exactly. So who's right?"

Aiden read the sign twice. He had assumed, all week, that the carbon dioxide came later, that the pyruvate sailed through the doorway intact and got broken apart somewhere down the hall in the Krebs cycle room, where all the dramatic chemistry happened. That was how he had memorized it, in order, tidily. But the sign said it plainly, and underneath the sign there was a physical model: a pyruvate going in one side, an acetyl-CoA coming out the other, and a little carbon dioxide spinning off between them, alone, first of its kind, released right there in the matrix.

"It's here," he said slowly. "It's this step. In the mitochondrial matrix, each pyruvate gets converted into acetyl-CoA, and that's where it releases one molecule of carbon dioxide. The first one. Marcus was right, which is going to be unbearable."

Elisa came over and looked at the model, tilting her head. "So Krebs makes carbon dioxide too, just not the first."

"Right, Krebs makes plenty, later. But the first one comes off here, before any of that." Aiden took a photo of the sign. He liked that it was slightly annoying, honestly. He had built the whole pathway in his head like a clean assembly line, and the truth was that the first little puff of carbon escaped in a transitional room he had barely bothered to memorize, in a doorway he'd been speeding through. The recalcitrant fact had refused to sit where he'd put it.

Samantha stopped filming. "Okay but wait, should we double check? Signs can be wrong. My little brother's museum has a sign that says Pluto is a planet."

"Your brother's museum is a lobby with a globe in it," said Elisa.

"It has a gift shop, Elisa."

Aiden pulled up his textbook on his phone, the deterrrence against Samantha's brother's museum standards, and scrolled to the chapter. There it was again, same words, same doorway, one carbon dioxide per pyruvate, released in the matrix when pyruvate became acetyl-CoA. He turned the phone around so they could both see it, feeling oddly triumphant, as if he had caught the fact in the wild twice.

"So Marcus gets to be right," Samantha said, deflating onto the kidney bench next to Elisa. "He's going to do that thing where he brings it up for a week."

"Let him," Aiden said. "We'll be right about everything else." He queued the video back to the beginning and stood up straight under the glucose chandelier, clearing his throat like a museum docent. "Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to The Power Plant. Please keep your hands inside the cell at all times."

"Start over," said Samantha, filming again, "and this time say matrix."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The derivative of a function at a point equals the slope of the line tangent to its graph at that point.
story:
Blake had told his mother the tutoring centre was a waste of the money she didn't have, and she had signed him up anyway, which was the kind of thing that passed for a compromise between them. The room smelled of dry-erase marker and old carpet. Six desks, a photocopied poster of the quadratic formula curling at one corner, and at the front, Ms. Teo, who ran the place with a red pen and no mercy. What Blake wanted was simple: a 78 on Friday's test, high enough to keep him in the running for the engineering stream, which was the whole reason he'd dropped music in September. He still wasn't sure that trade had been right. Some nights he could hear his old practice room in his head, the piano's low E going flat, and he would lie there doing derivative problems instead, as if the numbers could subsume the sound.

The topic was maxima. He sat hunched over a worksheet with the function f of x equals x cubed minus twelve x, and the instructions said to find where the value was greatest and prove it. He'd done the mechanical part twice already, but something about it bothered him, the way the algebra seemed to float free of anything he could picture. Ms. Teo had passed his desk and drawn one circle around his answer, which could mean anything.

At the desk beside him, Justin was not doing the worksheet. Justin had laid a ruler against the graph paper where he'd plotted the curve, tilting it slowly, watching where it touched the plotted points.

"What are you even doing," Blake said, not quite a question.

"Checking you," Justin said. "At your x equals two, I'm putting the ruler so it just touches the curve there, not cutting through it. A tangent line, that's called. Then I read the slope off the grid."

"That's not math," Blake said. "That's arts and crafts."

"That's the whole point," Justin said. "The derivative at a point equals the slope of the tangent line to the graph at that point. Same thing. One's a formula, one's a ruler." He held the ruler steady against the plotted curve near x equals two and counted squares. "Slope's coming out zero there. Flat. What'd you get?"

Blake looked at his own work. He had found the derivative, three x squared minus twelve, set it to zero, and gotten x equals two and x equals negative two. His slope at two was zero. He hadn't thought of it as flat, though; he'd thought of it as the answer.

"It's flat," he said slowly.

"At the top," Justin said. "That's your maximum, the peak of the curve. The tangent line there is horizontal." He slid the ruler to the other point, the valley at negative two, and tilted it level again. "Same flatness here, but it's the bottom. So the derivative alone doesn't tell you which is which. You have to look."

Blake had spent three years believing math was the part of school where you couldn't be lied to, where you followed the procedure and the procedure protected you. Somewhere in there he had also started to believe the procedure was all there was. Now Justin's ruler, this recalcitrant plastic thing with the millimetre markings worn off at one end, was telling him the same truth his algebra had, and the two versions refused to be ranked. He'd dismissed Justin in September as a jock slumming in calculus. He was aware of the unfairness of that now, arriving late and unearned, the way Lindsey had told him his apologies always did.

Lindsey looked over from the far desk, where she'd been arguing with a word problem about a fence. "Blake's having a revelation," she announced, with the elocution of someone doing a nature documentary. "The wild student discovers geometry."

"Shut up," Blake said, but without heat.

Ms. Teo came and stood behind them. Blake tensed for the lecture, the explanation he'd have to nod along to, but she only looked at the ruler for a long moment and then at his worksheet. "Show me how you'd know the peak is a peak and not a valley," she said, and waited. She did this, he'd noticed; she refused to give you anything you could reach yourself.

"Left of two the slope is negative," Blake said, tracing the curve with his pencil. "Right of two it's positive. So it goes up, flattens, comes down. That's a maximum." He heard himself say it and found he believed it in two ways at once, the numbers and the shape, and that neither one by itself had convinced him until now.

"Good," Ms. Teo said, and moved on.

He stayed after the others left. The centre was closing in twenty minutes and the fluorescent lights had begun their faint evening buzz, but he kept plotting points, kept laying the ruler against the curve, watching the slope tilt from steep to flat to steep again. He thought about the piano again, about whether choosing one thing had to mean abandoning the other, or whether, like the formula and the ruler, they could both be true of the same curve. He didn't know. He put the ruler in his backpack anyway, next to the pencil case, where it would be on Friday.

"Lock up when you go," Ms. Teo called from the doorway, and he nodded, still counting squares.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: ATP synthase works like a tiny rotary motor: protons flowing through it make part of the enzyme spin, and that motion builds ATP.
story:
Rachel spread the diagram across the picnic table in her backyard and weighted its corners with her mother's gardening stones, because the textbook would not stay open and because refusing to admit that felt like a kind of weakness. Glucose sat at the top of the page in a neat hexagon, and below it, arrows fanned out through stages with names she could recite but not quite picture. Glycolysis, the link reaction, the cycle. The final arrow vanished into a drawing of a mitochondrion, cross-sectioned like a littoral zone on a map of some country she had never visited, inner and outer banks folded around each other.

The problem was Tuesday. On Tuesday there was a retake, and the retake existed because Rachel had gone into the original exam knowing that glucose became energy and had written, with great confidence, that the mitochondria "absorbed" it, like a cell taking a snack. Mr. Littlechild had circled the sentence in red and written "See me" beside it, which was the least reassuring pair of words in the English language. She had seen him. He had not lectured. He had asked her one question, which was how she thought the cell stored the energy if not in lumps, and she had not been able to answer, and he had said, "Then don't memorize it. Find out how it actually works, and tell me Thursday."

Meriem arrived through the back gate with a bag of cherries and Amira behind her, arguing about a museum. Amira had been to the science museum in the city over the weekend, the one with the giant walk-through heart, and she would not stop describing a smaller exhibit on a lower floor, a motor made of colored plastic that turned and turned. "It was labeled ATP synthase," she said, pronouncing it carefully, twice, as if the name were a spell. "There was a handle, like a turbine. And a sign that said protons flowing through it make part of the enzyme spin."

Rachel put down her pen. "Spin."

"Spin. Like this." Amira held up a cherry stem between two fingers and twirled it. "And the spinning builds ATP. That's what the sign said. I took a picture, but the flash ruined it."

Meriem said the museum was for children, which was her way of admitting she had wanted to go. Rachel pulled the textbook diagram closer and found the small mushroom-shaped shape embedded in the inner membrane of the mitochondrion, the one she had skipped past because it looked decorative. It was labeled with the same name Amira had said. She had been reading past it for two weeks.

"Okay," she said slowly. "So the whole arrow at the end, the part I kept memorizing, the electron transport chain, all of that is pumping protons across this membrane. Like filling a water tower. And then they can only get back through this one thing." She tapped the mushroom. "And when they flow through it, part of it turns."

"A tiny rotary motor," Amira said, and twirled the stem again, and this time Meriem watched it, and the three of them were quiet in the way people are quiet when something has just clicked into place and no one wants to jinx it.

Rachel tried to explain it back, hands moving. The glucose got broken down in stages, nothing dramatic, step after step, and the last stage used that slow dismantling to push protons to one side of the membrane until the imbalance itself was the energy, waiting. Then protons flowed through ATP synthase, made it spin, and the motion built ATP. "It's not a lump," she said. "It's a wheel. The cell doesn't store dinner, it stores water pressure." She was aware that this was not quite right either, that "water pressure" was her own metaphor and metaphors were how she had gotten into trouble the first time, but it was closer, and being closer felt like something she could stand on.

Meriem, spitting cherry pits into the grass, offered the observation that the mitochondrion had probably once been a separate bacterium living inside another cell, and that the whole arrangement was ancient symbiosis, two things merging so long ago that nobody remembered the merger. Rachel said she didn't need that for Tuesday. Meriem said she didn't need it either, she just liked it. Amira said that if the textbook wanted students to understand motors, it should print a motor, not a paragraph, and Rachel said the paragraph was fine now, actually, now that she had seen the shape of the thing in Amira's cherry stem.

The light moved across the table and the gardening stones held the corners down and Rachel copied the whole pathway onto one sheet of paper from memory, glucose at the top, arrows descending, the spinning shape at the end with the word ATP synthase printed beside it in her small careful capitals. There was still a piece she was unsure of, which was why the protons wanted to flow back at all, whether that was wanting, whether the word "want" belonged anywhere in a sentence about a membrane. She wrote a question mark in the margin beside it. She would keep the question mark. It seemed more honest than erasing it, and if Mr. Littlechild asked her on Thursday what she still didn't know, she wanted to have an answer ready.

Amira held out the bag of cherries. Rachel took two, put the pits in her pocket for lack of a better plan, and went inside to find her flashcards, and through the screen door Meriem called, "Tell him about the symbiosis anyway."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Research on homesickness finds that nearly everyone away from home misses something about it, and roughly 20 percent of university students rate theirs at or above the midpoint of a severity scale.
story:
