Lauren sat on the floor of her half-empty bedroom with a roll of packing tape across her knees, and the room had reached the stage where it looked less like a bedroom than like an argument between two versions of itself. Against one wall, the boxes were neat and labeled in her mother's handwriting, which was small and certain. Against the other, everything Lauren had refused to pack yet was heaped in a soft pile: the string lights Anais had given her for her fifteenth birthday, a shoebox of notes from sophomore year, a dried corsage she could not remember wearing.

She had promised herself she would be efficient about this. Her father, who thought of himself as a practical man, had given her a bombastic speech at dinner about how the family that labels its boxes survives the move, and she had internalized the lesson for approximately one day before reverting to sitting among her things and deciding, one object at a time, what deserved to come. The trouble was that deciding felt like ranking. The string lights could not be more important than the notes, and if they were equally important, then why was she ranking at all.

Her phone buzzed against the carpet. Anais again.

Did you decide about Friday? Alana says come anyway, even if it's sad. Her word, not mine.

Lauren typed, deleted, typed again. Friday was the going-away thing at Alana's house, a party that nobody was calling a party, and Lauren had been circling it for a week the way you circle a cold lake. She wanted to go and she wanted to already have gone, to have it behind her, the hugging and the toasts and the photos taken by someone's mother in the doorway. She wrote, I'll come, and then put the phone face down on the carpet as though it might take the answer back.

Through the window she could see Mr. Wanjiru next door, watering his tomatoes in the late sun the way he had done every evening of her childhood. He was the one who had taught her to deadhead the roses, and he was the reason she had lasted three weeks in the community garden club before deciding she lacked the temperament. "You're not a misanthrope," he had told her then, amused. "You just prefer plants to committees." She could admit now, watching him bend to a tomato with the care of a man lifting a sleeping child, that she had liked being let off the hook by that sentence. It was easier to believe she was a certain kind of person than to keep showing up and finding out she wasn't.

Her mother called up the stairs that dinner was in twenty minutes. Lauren answered, "Okay," and did not move. She opened the shoebox instead.

The notes were folded into triangles, mostly from Anais, some from Alana, a few from people she had not thought about in two years, which felt like a small betrayal of them. On top was one from the fall of junior year, when Anais had come back from visiting her sister at university and had been strange for a week, quiet at lunch, snapping at small things. Lauren had assumed it was about a boy. She found the note now, Anais's round handwriting flattened by the fold: Thanks for not asking what was wrong until I could say it.

She had never actually found out what had been wrong. She smoothed the note against her thigh and texted Anais directly, skipping the group thread.

That week you got back from your sister's school junior year. What was that about?

The reply came slowly enough that Lauren packed three books while she waited.

I was homesick. For here, I mean. I was only visiting her for four days and I missed my own house so much it was embarrassing. I thought something was wrong with me.

Lauren sat back on her heels. She typed, It was four days, and deleted it, because it sounded like an accusation.

Anais sent another message before she could compose anything kinder. I looked it up after, actually. Research on homesickness finds that nearly everyone away from home misses something about it. And around twenty percent of university students rate their homesickness at or above the midpoint of a severity scale. I made my sister quiz me on it in the car.

Lauren read it twice. She had been thinking of her own move, two hundred miles in August, as a test of independence she might fail, and she had assumed the test was silent, that whatever weakness it exposed would be hers alone. But if nearly everyone missed something, then missing something was not the result of the test. It was the weather the test happened in. And if one in five students rated theirs at or above that midpoint, then there was a scale somewhere, a real one, and some people measured higher on it, and nobody she knew had ever said so out loud except Anais, who had needed a week and a sister and a car ride to say it even to herself.

So it's normal, Lauren sent.

Normal and sometimes serious, Anais sent back. Those aren't the same thing. My sister says the serious kind you actually deal with, like a thing with numbers on it.

Lauren looked at the pile of things she had refused to pack. She thought about going to Alana's on Friday and standing in the doorway for the photos, and about August, a dorm room she had seen only in pictures, a roommate she had texted twice. She did not know yet which kind she would be, the kind who missed a little or the kind who missed by half the scale. Maybe you couldn't know in advance. Maybe knowing the scale existed was the part you could do from a bedroom floor in June.

Her mother called again, softer this time, and Lauren could hear that she had come to the bottom of the stairs.

Down in a minute, Lauren called. She put Anais's note in the box marked KEEP, on top of the string lights, and tore off a strip of tape.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: German capitalizes every noun, not only names, which helps a reader of a German article spot the nouns in a sentence at a glance.
story:
Hannah had promised her host mother she would read one article from the local paper and summarize it at breakfast, in German, aloud, and breakfast was in eleven hours. The paper lay folded on the desk of the little room above the bakery, and the article she had chosen was four paragraphs long, which had seemed manageable at noon and now looked like a wall. She copied the first sentence into her notebook and stared at it: so many of the words began with capital letters, in the middle of the sentence, where capitals had no business being.

There was a knock, and Alexandre leaned in without waiting. He was the neighbor's son, seventeen, and he had appointed himself her guide to the town, a role he performed by walking slightly ahead of her and gesturing at things. "You look like someone preparing for arbitration," he said, dropping onto the bed. "Who is suing whom?"

"I have to summarize this at breakfast and I don't even know which words matter. Half of them are capitalized. Why is that word capitalized? It's in the middle of the sentence." She pointed at a word in the second line.

"German capitalizes every noun, not only names," Alexandre said, with a shrug that suggested this was the least interesting fact in the world. "So the nouns announce themselves. You see them coming."

She looked down at the sentence again, and the page changed shape in her hands. The capitalized words stood up out of the line like people raising hands in a classroom: the noun, the noun, the noun, strung along the sentence with lowercase words between them, the verbs and the little connective words she mostly recognized. She could not yet read the sentence, exactly, but she could suddenly see its skeleton. She wrote the capitalized words in a column down the margin and found she had, without translating anything, a list of what the article was about: the bridge, the money, the council, the delay.

Alexandre, meanwhile, had begun to pontificate about the bridge, and she let him, because his pontificating was also practice. The bridge in the article, it emerged, was the one they had crossed that afternoon, the footbridge over the canal, and it was going to be closed for repairs starting Monday. The town council had argued about it for months. He delivered this as a prolix complaint about politicians and bicycles, and she caught perhaps one word in five, but she caught "Monday," and she caught the name of the bridge, because it was capitalized too, like everything else that mattered.

At dinner, the host mother asked how the article was going, and Hannah said it was going, and did not mention the column of nouns. She wanted to see, first, whether the column actually held. After dinner she worked through the second paragraph with the paper dictionary, and the paragraph turned out not to be about the schedule of repairs at all. It was about a retired teacher, Ms. Georgiou, who had written to the paper arguing that closing the footbridge during the school term was a mistake, that the children from the eastern streets would have to walk forty minutes around the canal. The council's answer was in the fourth paragraph, and it was a paragraph of nothing, of process and committees, and Hannah recognized the shape of it even in a language she barely had. Some sentences were the same in every country.

She went down to the kitchen for water and found the host mother still at the table, reading the same paper, and there was a silence in the room that had weight to it. "You found the article about the bridge," the host mother said at last, not a question. Hannah said yes, she had. "My mother lives on the eastern side," the host mother said. "Ms. Georgiou was my teacher." She turned the page, and turned it back, and did not say anything else, and Hannah understood that the breakfast summary was not going to be only an exercise in German. She was going to stand at the table and describe, out loud, in front of this woman, an argument that touched this house.

In the morning she was nervous enough that she kept her notebook under the table edge, but she did not look at it. She began badly, dropped a word, picked it up. She said that the article was about the footbridge over the canal, and that the council wanted to close it Monday for repairs, and that Ms. Georgiou had written to the paper to say that the children from the eastern streets would walk forty minutes around the canal if they closed it during the school term. Her German was slow and her grammar was wrong in at least two places, and she could hear it, and she kept going. The nouns carried her, the ones that had stood up out of the page last night, each one with its capital letter like a raised hand.

When she finished, the host mother was quiet for a moment, then said, "Forty minutes," and poured Hannah's coffee, and Hannah could not tell whether that was approval or grief or both, and did not ask. Later, walking to meet Alexandre at the corner, Hannah crossed the footbridge and stopped in the middle of it, where the canal was green and still and the bakery smell came up warm through the boards beneath her feet. She took out her phone and photographed the far bank, the eastern streets, the long way around, and put the phone away unshared, undecided what she would do with it.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In the UK, a driver who passes the test in an automatic car may drive only automatic cars, and must pass a manual test to drive a manual car.
story:
Anna had the keys in her fist before the instructor's car even turned the corner, which was the first mistake of the morning, though nobody had told her that yet. The driveway was long and grey and bordered by her mother's roses, and at the top of it sat the family car, a battered manual Golf that her father referred to, with reverence, as "the last honest machine in this house." Anna had signed up for automatic lessons anyway. She had done it quietly, the way you do anything you suspect your family will treat as a moral failing, and she had planned to tell them after.

"You're early," said Mitchell, unfolding himself from the driving school's little blue car with a clipboard and the smug posture of someone who had passed his test four months ago and had not yet stopped mentioning it. "I'm your instructor. Surprise. Ms. Liu had a dentist thing." He was seventeen two months ago and this was technically legal and Anna felt the ground shift slightly. "Buckle up. We'll do the driveway, then the estate roads, then, if you don't kill us, the retail park, which is where souls go to coagulate."

"That's not what that word means."

"It's exactly what it means. Have you seen a retail park on a Saturday?"

Anna got in, adjusted the seat, checked her mirrors with the exaggerated care of a girl performing diligence. The automatic was easy, insultingly easy, the pedal doing all the thinking. By the third lap of the driveway she was almost bored, and boredom made her honest. "My dad's going to have opinions about this car," she said, nodding at the Golf as they rolled past it. "Three pedals. He thinks automatics are moral laziness. He calls the clutch a character-building exercise. Like asceticism, but with your left foot."

Mitchell laughed, then stopped laughing in a way Anna noticed. "You do know, right? If you pass in an automatic, that's it. You can only drive automatics. You'd have to pass a whole other test to drive that thing." He pointed at the Golf as if introducing it. "Manual test. Separate one."

"That's insane."

"That's the law. Ask Melodie, she looked it up for a week because her nan's got an automatic and her mum's got a manual and she was deciding which side of the family to be loyal to."

Anna drove another slow lap while this settled. The driveway looked different now, narrower, hedged in by consequences. She had wanted the easy road and could admit it; she had also, apparently, wanted to borrow the Golf for the sixth-form road trip in September without ever saying so out loud, even to herself, and the two wants had just collided with the sound of a small legal fact. "So the automatic is easier," she said slowly, "and the manual is harder now but freer later, and there's no clever third option where I get both. That's a genuinely annoying design."

"Welcome to being an adult. It's mostly that."

From the kitchen window, Ms. Liu watched the little blue car crawl past the roses for what must have been the ninth time. She had come back from the dentist early, half her face still numb, and had decided against interrupting. She recognised the girl's posture at the wheel, the over-corrected mirrors, and she recognised something else too: the way Anna kept glancing at the Golf. Ms. Liu had owned a manual car once, years ago, and had never learned to drive it. She'd passed her test in an automatic, then discovered that her licence covered automatics only, and the manual had sat in her own driveway like a promise she'd made in a language she couldn't speak, until she sold it to a man who drove it away in under a minute. She had never told anyone that. It was the kind of thing that coagulated, if you let it, into shame, and she had mostly not let it.

She carried two mugs of tea out anyway, because a driveway lesson without tea was, in her view, a failed lesson. "How's she doing?" she asked Mitchell, in the tone of a neutral observer.

"Suspiciously well," Mitchell said. "She found out about the automatic licence thing and instead of crying she started muttering about trade-offs. I think she's going to be fine. Or a philosopher. Possibly both."

Anna rolled down the window. Her face was set in the expression Ms. Liu knew from chess club, three moves deep and annoyed about the fourth. "Ms. Liu. You've driven for years. If you passed in an automatic, could you drive that?" She pointed at the Golf.

Ms. Liu considered the numb left side of her face, the driveway, the roses, and thirty years of careful silence. "No," she said. "I couldn't. I'd have to pass another test first. A manual one."

"You drive an automatic."

"I drive an automatic."

The tea steamed. Mitchell looked from one woman to the other with the delight of someone watching a twist he hadn't written. Anna put the car in park, very gently, and turned in her seat.

"Ms. Liu," she said, "would you like to learn clutch control in my dad's car, in this driveway, badly, with me coaching from the passenger seat based on zero experience?"

Ms. Liu took a sip of tea, then handed the mug to Mitchell, who received it like a sceptre.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under US federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant.
story:
The application had forty-one questions, and Alice answered them all at the kitchen table while her mother made soup and offered commentary. "Availability," her mother read over her shoulder. "Write anytime. Eager but not desperate." Alice wrote Saturday and Sunday and after four on weekdays, which was the truth, and turned in the form at Halloran's Grocery the next afternoon. By Friday she had an interview, and by Sunday a polo shirt in a shade of green that Mckenzie, over video call, described as "the exact color of a crayon nobody ever uses."

"My first job," Alice said, holding the shirt up to the camera. "I'm going to be transfigured. Responsible. Odorous of turkey."

"Odorous is not a word you want associated with your transformation," Mckenzie said, "and also I don't think it's a word."

It was a word, Alice confirmed later, though the dictionary example was about garbage. Her first shift was Tuesday, four to eight, and consisted mostly of learning where the mop lived and being introduced to the deli case by a woman named Dolores, who had worked at Halloran's for twenty-two years and narrated the cold cuts like they were personal friends. "Capocolano, sweet ham, olive loaf, which nobody buys but I refuse to retire." Behind Dolores, gleaming and terrible, stood the slicer, a machine the size of a small horse with a blade like a silent moon.

Thursday, Dolores called in sick. The manager, a peevish man named Rick who seemed to hold the flu personally against Dolores, found Alice restocking the pickle jars. "You're on the deli," he said. "Sandwiches, and slice whatever the ticket says. It's easy. You'll figure it out."

Alice looked toward the slicer, which caught the fluorescent light and returned it coldly. "I can do the sandwiches," she said. "But I can't run the slicer. I'm seventeen."

"So? Dolores will show you sometime."

"It's not a training thing. Under federal child labor rules, workers under eighteen can't operate power-driven meat slicers. Even in a grocery store deli. Or a restaurant."

Rick made a face like she had recited a limerick at him. "Everyone starts on the slicer."

"Not everyone under eighteen," Alice said. "Legally, no one under eighteen. Federal." She had read the whole fact the night before, partly out of nerves and partly because her neighbor Ms. Pereira, who had arranged the interview in the first place, had told her the single most useful thing about any job: know what you're not allowed to do before someone asks you to do it. Alice had assumed this meant lifting with your knees.

"Fine," Rick said, after a silence in which he appeared to be negotiating with the concept of federal law and losing. "You take the counter. I'll pull Gene from produce."

Gene turned out to be sixty and delighted, since produce was cold and the deli had a stool. For the next three hours Alice built sandwiches under his supervision while he sliced roast beef and told her about his hot air balloon phase, which had ended, he said, "under duress, from my wife and also the FAA." A woman ordered a pound of provolone, paper thin, and watched Gene's hands with the reverence of someone at church.

At eight, Alice clocked out and called Mckenzie from the parking lot. "I said no to my boss on my third shift."

" Fired?"

"Promoted, possibly, to nothing. Gene from produce loves me. I made him a sandwich with everything because he paid for it and then forgot he paid and paid again, and I had to chase him with a refund like a tiny lawyer."

She sat on the curb after, in the green polo, still holding the refund receipt she'd failed to give Gene because he'd driven away waving her off. It was possible, she thought, that she'd been right and also that Rick would quietly give the weekend shifts to someone less complicated. Both could be true at once. Her phone buzzed: Rick, a text that read, Saturday 4-8, deli counter, don't touch the slicer, Gene will slice.

She typed back a thumbs up, then deleted it and typed, "Understood. Thanks, Rick," because she was trying on being a person with a job, one who didn't end every exchange with an emoji. Then she got in her mother's car, still smelling faintly of provolone, and drove home past Ms. Pereira's porch, where the porch light was on like a small applause.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Binary search needs to jump straight to the middle item, so it loses its advantage on a linked list, where reaching the middle means walking through the items one by one.
story:
The canoe racks behind the dining hall had been converted into a whiteboard, and Ms. Otieno had written one word on it in green marker: SEARCH. "You have a sorted list of a thousand names," she said. "How do you find one?" Leonard, who had claimed the driest log and was eating blueberries with insouciant devotion, raised a hand without looking up. "Start at the top and read until you get there." "That's a linear search," she said. "It works. Now make it faster."

Elliot had come to this coding week at camp because his older brother had told him that everything worth learning would be learned the hard way, and because Oceane had come, and because the lake was right there. He had not expected to spend the first afternoon sweating over a laptop on a picnic table while wasps investigated his lemonade. But by dinner he had it: check the middle item first, decide whether the target is above or below, throw away the half that can't hold it, and repeat. Ten guesses could cover a thousand names, because each guess halved what remained. He showed Oceane, who tilted her head at his screen like a bird examining something shiny.

"That can't be legal," she said. "It's not chicanery," Elliot said. "It's arithmetic. The list has to be sorted, that's the price." She pushed his elbow off the table. "Then prove it. Beat me." They each wrote a program to find a name in a sorted list of ten thousand. Hers walked the list item by item; his jumped to the middle. His finished so fast the timer couldn't measure it. Leonard wandered over, looked at both screens, and said, "Elliot's is witchcraft," which Elliot decided to take as a compliment.

That night the boys in Cabin 4 stayed up arguing about whether aliens would know binary search, and Elliot lay on his bunk and cogitated on the deeper question, which was not speed but structure. He had a phone book of a mind full of facts about the day, and he kept checking the middle of it: Oceane had laughed at his joke at lunch and had not sat with him at dinner. He fell asleep without deciding which half of the evidence to throw away.

The next morning brought the humbling. Ms. Otieno gave them a new assignment: the camp's muster list, stored as a linked list, each camper's name pointing to the next like beads on a string, because the waterfront staff added and removed names constantly and a linked list made that painless. "Find Marisol," she said. Elliot grinned, opened his code, and dropped his binary search in. He set it running and leaned back to enjoy his own cleverness.

The program crawled. It found Marisol, eventually, in roughly the same time Oceane's dumb, honest, linear search did. He ran both again, and again, and the numbers refused to be dramatic. Leonard leaned over his shoulder. "Witchcraft's broken," Leonard said. Elliot stared at the screen, and then at the structure Ms. Otieno had drawn on the whiteboard, arrows in a patient line, no jumping allowed. He tested it, because he didn't trust himself to reason while embarrassed. He told his program to find the middle of the linked list and counted what it did to get there. It walked. Item by item, bead by bead, from the first name to the middle, every single time, before it could even make its first clever guess. The middle wasn't a place you could jump to; it was a place you had to walk to, and after walking there you had to walk somewhere else to halve the remainder.

"Binary search needs to jump straight to the middle item," he said slowly, mostly to himself, "so it loses its advantage on a linked list, where reaching the middle means walking through the items one by one." Oceane, who had been quietly filling a water bottle, set it down. "So your fast search is only fast if you can jump." "Right. The data has to let you jump, or the halving is a lie." He said it with the flat voice of someone watching his own cleverness get handed back to him, receipt attached.

He tried fixing it. He built an array alongside the linked list, an index of pointers, so the jumps could happen in the index even if the names lived on the string. It worked; the search got fast again; and it cost him the entire lunch period plus a mistake where he swapped two campers' cabin assignments and a nine-year-old named Dov ended up scheduled for the senior overnight hike. Ms. Otieno found the error before the buses loaded, fixed it with two keystrokes, and gave Elliot a look he would remember through at least his first semester of college.

He never did settle whether the trade was worth it, the index against the walking, and he said so at the final demo, standing in front of the whiteboard with green marker dust on his fingers. "It's faster," he said. "Whether it's better depends on how much the staff adds names, and I don't know that yet." Oceane caught his eye from the second row. "So test it," she said. "Tomorrow. Before breakfast." He nodded, closed the laptop lid, and they walked down toward the lake, the last light flat and gold on the water.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The secret printed ballot is called the Australian ballot because Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856.
story:
The ballot came in a plain envelope, and Samantha carried it from the mailbox to the kitchen table the way she carried her acceptance letters, flat against her chest, as though a gust could spoil it. She had turned eighteen nine days before the election, which felt engineered, like the universe had cleared its throat at exactly the right moment.

At the kitchen table she laid out the papers and two pens, because the first pen might fail, and got her phone out. Mia had texted her three times that morning, all caps, about the school board candidate, the one who had promised to protect the arts program. Rowen had answered the group chat with a single screenshot of that same candidate's voting record on the transit levy, which had nothing to do with anything, except that it did, somehow, because Rowen always found the angle nobody else had thought to check. Samantha had spent the weekend between them like a person standing in a doorway between two rooms, both lit differently.

Her father came through with laundry and paused at her shoulder. "You want privacy for that?"

"Do I?"

"That's the whole point, I think." He put the basket down. "Nobody's allowed to see how you mark it."

That was the piece she'd looked up on Thursday, at one in the morning, when she should have been asleep. The secret printed ballot was called the Australian ballot, she had read, because the Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856. She had been genuinely surprised, sitting there with her chin on her fist. Australia. She had assumed secrecy was as old as voting itself, some clause in the founding of everything, and instead it was an invention, a reform, younger than the photograph. When she'd told Mia this on the bus, Mia had said, "Wait, so before that people just watched each other vote?" and Samantha had said, "Basically," and had felt, briefly, like the kind of person who knew things. Her father would like it too, but she saved it. She wanted to tell Mr. Walker, who had voted in eleven elections or so and who kept his opinions to himself so completely that Samantha had once suspected he was guarding something. The suspicion had proved wrong, but the habit of wondering about him hadn't left.

Before she could tell anyone anything, though, there was the actual ballot, and the actual pen, and the actual circle to fill in. She read the school board race twice. The candidate Mia wanted was an aesthete in the loosest sense, a woman who quoted poets at council meetings and wore good scarves; Rowen found her unserious; Samantha found her sincere in a way that was hard to fake and possibly easy to perform, and the distinction between those two things kept dissolving the closer she looked. She filled in no circle. She drank some water. She looked at the window, where the first yellow leaves on the neighbor's maple had begun to presage the whole gray month to come, and thought about how her mother had once told her, over dishes, that she had sat out one election in her twenties because she couldn't decide and felt that an equivocal vote was worse than none. Samantha had argued with her then, fifteen years old and certain. Now she was less certain, which felt like a demotion and also, strangely, like being let in on something.

She went across the street to Mr. Walker's porch with the sealed inner envelope still in her jacket, needing a walk more than an answer. He was oiling the hinges on his screen door, and he asked if she'd voted yet, and she said she'd voted in her head but not on paper.

"There's a difference," he said.

"I know. That's the problem." She sat on his step. "Did you know the secret ballot has a name? It's called the Australian ballot. Tasmania and Victoria introduced it in 1856. The colonies."

"Is that right."

"You didn't know that."

"I didn't," he said, and tested the hinge, and the door swung quiet, and he seemed pleased by both things.

She told him about Mia and Rowen, the scarves and the screenshot, the circle she hadn't filled. He didn't advise her. He said the election he remembered best was one where he'd changed his mind in the booth itself, pen in hand, and that he'd never fully settled whether that had been wisdom or cowardice arriving late. He said it evenly, without weight, which made it heavier. Samantha thought of her mother at the sink, her hands still in the water, the confession offered like it cost a little even after all the years. Both of them, standing in doorways between rooms.

Back at her kitchen table the light had gone long and orange. She picked up the first pen, and it did fail, a dry scratch across the circle, and she had to request a fresh ink cartridge of herself, breathe, take the second pen. She filled in the school board circle. Then, before she could seal the inner envelope, her father came through again with the laundry, and she turned the paper face down on the table without deciding to, fast, and heard herself say, "It's called the Australian ballot, by the way. Nobody's allowed to see how you mark it. Tasmania and Victoria, 1856."

"Then stop hovering," she added, and he laughed and left, and she slid the ballot into the envelope, folded the flap, and pressed it flat with the heel of her hand.

She was halfway to the mailbox at the corner when she realized she couldn't remember, with any confidence, whether the circle she'd darkened was Mia's candidate or the other one. She stood at the box with the flag down, mail slot open, and held the envelope under the streetlight. The glue was already set. Somewhere behind her, Mr. Walker's screen door opened without a sound.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Biotech billionaire Patrick Soon-Shiong bought the Los Angeles Times in 2018 for $500 million, plus the assumption of pension obligations.
story:
Jessica had been trying to print the same paragraph for ten minutes, and the printer kept producing sheets with a gray bar across the middle, like the machine was censoring itself. The student newspaper office, a converted storage room behind the gym, smelled of toner and the cold pizza Naomie kept in the mini fridge for emergencies she never defined.

"Try tray two," Naomie said, without looking up from her layout screen. "It only jams on tray one when it's humid, and it's always humid in here."

Jessica fed the paper into tray two and thought, not for the first time, that the printer was the most honest thing in the room. It refused. The paper refused to come out clean. She was writing a piece about the school board's new contract with a food vendor, and every question she asked seemed to curve back toward somebody's pocket.

The trouble had started at dinner two nights before. Her father, folding and unfolding his napkin, had said that all newspapers were dying and the only ones that survived were rescued by rich men. Her mother had laughed, not unkindly. "Rescued," she said. "Or bought." They had gone back and forth about the Los Angeles Times, which their cousin in California still read. Jessica had looked it up afterward, at her desk, with her notebook open: a biotech billionaire named Patrick Soon-Shiong bought the Los Angeles Times in 2018 for 500 million dollars, plus the assumption of pension obligations. She read the phrase twice. She liked how the money and the pensions sat in the same sentence, one loud, one quiet, like a man carrying a suitcase in one hand and somebody's grandmother in the other.

That was the word she kept turning over. Bought. Not donated to, not endowed. Bought.

"Earth to Jessica," Naomie said. "Your face does a thing when you're interrogating a word. It's like watching a cat decide about a cucumber."

"That's fear, not curiosity."

"Same posture."

Mariane came in with her camera bag and the particular walk of someone carrying news. "You two will want to hear this," she said. She set the bag down on the pizza box, which was apparently furniture now. "I was shooting the vendor tasting in the cafeteria, and the principal pulled me aside. Very friendly. Very interested in my future. Did I know the vendor's regional manager was a major donor to the district foundation? Did I think it was fair to, quote, insinuate things about a company that supports our schools?"

Jessica sat back. "What did you say?"

"I said I was seventeen and my camera doesn't insinuate, it exposes. Which he did not love." Mariane grinned, then let it fade. "He also mentioned our printing budget gets renewed by the district every spring. Just mentioned it."

The printer groaned and produced a clean page at last, and Jessica picked it up and held it against the light, as if the gray bar might reappear. She thought about her parents' argument, which had ended unresolved, both of them refilling their tea. Her father had said a rich owner saves a newspaper that would otherwise fold. Her mother had said the question isn't whether he saves it, it's what it costs to be saved. Jessica had thought, lying awake, that both of them were right and both of them were certain, and the certainty was the part she didn't trust.

She had flashed back all week to eighth grade, when the school had renamed the library after a donor and quietly removed three shelves of books about labor unions, or maybe the shelves had just been weeded for age, and no one ever established which. Even then she had wondered: how would a person find out? Who kept the list of what was removed? She hadn't wondered hard enough to ask. That was the thing about being twelve; the questions dissolved before the bell.

"Here's what I keep circling," she said now, pulling her chair toward the others. "The Los Angeles Times got bought for five hundred million dollars, plus the assumption of pension obligations. That's real. The man is a biotech billionaire, and he owns it. And the paper still runs stories. Some of them probably hard ones. So ownership isn't a light switch. It's more like, I don't know, weather."

"Weather," Naomie repeated.

"Yeah. It shapes everything, but it doesn't decide every single thing. And you can't point at one cloud and say, that's why it rained." She laughed at herself. "I just compared media criticism to meteorology, which is going to look incredible in my college essay."

Mariane pulled out her camera and started scrolling. "So what do we actually do? Because I have photos of the vendor's sample meals, and the contract, and now a principal who knows my name."

"We print," Jessica said. "But we do it like adults. We put the donation in the story, plainly, as a fact. We put the district's side in, at full length. And we run a box on page two explaining who funds us, and that our budget renews every spring, so readers can weigh that too."

"That box will make us look compromised."

"We are compromised," Jessica said. "Everybody's compromised by something. The Times has a billionaire, we have a school board, the principal has a donor. The question isn't whether you're leaning, it's whether you tell people which way the wind blows." She paused, hearing her mother's cadence in her own voice, and her father's too, which was strange and a little funny. "I'm not sure the metaphor survives daylight, but the principle might."

Naomie opened a blank page and typed a header: WHO PAYS FOR THIS PAPER. "Liminality," she said, apropos of nothing, which for Naomie meant a mood. "We're between being a school club and being journalists. It's the between-ness that's dangerous and fun."

The three of them worked until the hallway lights clicked off, and Jessica drafted the disclosure box twice, deleting a phrase about donors trying to burnish their image with school funding because she couldn't prove intent, only amounts. Undisclosed money could be deleterious to trust, she wrote instead, then crossed that out too, because it sounded like a vitamin label, and wrote: here is who pays us, and here is what they get, which is nothing except this sentence.

At nine, Ms. Kamau, the English teacher who signed off on their publication every month, knocked once and leaned in the doorway. She read the layout over Jessica's shoulder, the vendor story, the photos, the box on page two. She was quiet long enough that Jessica's stomach folded itself into a crane.

"Print it," Ms. Kamau said. "All of it." Then she pointed at the disclosure box. "Next month, tell them about the pizza too."

"The pizza?"

"Somebody's parents bought that oven for the club. Best two hundred dollars this school ever spent, and the students never once credited them."

Naomie was already typing. "Correction," she read aloud. "The mini fridge and pizza are provided by the Mariane family, who ask only for leftovers."

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In West Virginia v. Barnette (1943), the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance.
story:
Wyatt spread the briefs across the kitchen table, one stack for the school board, one for the student, and the lamplight made the crepuscular kitchen feel almost like a courtroom. Mr. Katz had assigned him both sides of the case for Thursday's mock court, and Wyatt had argued that this was a punishment disguised as an honor, though he had said it in more polite words. He was seventeen and had never before tried to hold two positions at once, the way you might hold two live wires, believing each one only when you held it.

His mother drifted through for tea and paused at the stacks. "You look like a lawyer already," she said, and set a cup beside him without being asked, the way she did when she could tell he had forgotten to drink anything since dinner.

"The hardest part isn't the arguing," Wyatt said. "It's arguing the other side like I mean it."

She tapped the school board stack. "Then mean it. Somebody has to, or you're just performing." She carried her tea toward the doorway, then turned back. "Isis called twice while you were at Luke's. Don't forget."

He hadn't forgotten. He had just been avoiding it, because Isis was arguing the student's side only, and she argued the way she breathed, continuously and with conviction, and Wyatt was afraid his divided loyalties would look like weakness to her.

Luke arrived first, though, knocking twice and letting himself in, a printout folded in his back pocket. He dropped into the chair across from Wyatt and slid the paper across the table. "Your whole petitioner brief is missing something," Luke said. "Check the last page."

Wyatt unfolded it. It was a case citation, photocopied from a textbook, the print small and dense. West Virginia v. Barnette, 1943. He read it twice. In West Virginia v. Barnette, 1943, the Supreme Court had ruled 6-3 that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance. He sat back slowly. Everything he had drafted for the school board's side assumed the school could compel the salute, and here was the Court, decades earlier, saying it could not.

"Where did you get this?"

"Isis gave it to me to give to you," Luke said. "She said you'd want to know before Thursday rather than after."

So Isis had not been calling to argue with him. She had been calling to save him. Wyatt felt the embarrassment arrive and then recede, replaced by something more like gratitude, and he picked up his phone.

When Isis answered, he said, "I found the Barnette thing. Thank you."

"You're welcome," she said. "Now do you understand why I was yelling on Saturday?"

"I understand it's settled. Schools can't force the salute or the pledge. Six to three."

"It's settled for forcing," Isis said. "Your side isn't forcing, though, is it? Read your own brief. Your school board is pressuring, encouraging, calling it civic duty. That's the game you have to play."

The kitchen had gone fully dark outside the windows, and Wyatt looked at the two stacks on the table and understood, for the first time, that they were not two arguments but two ideas about what a school was for. He worked until nearly midnight, and his mother came down once in her robe and set a plate of bread and cheese beside him, saying nothing, and he ate it without noticing until it was gone.

What Wyatt discovered, drafting the school board's side with Barnette in view, was that the case did not destroy his argument so much as sharpen it. He could not claim the power to compel, so he had to claim the power to persuade, and persuasion, he admitted to himself at two in the morning, was not nothing. A school asked things of students all day. Stand for the teacher. Silence in the halls. The question was where asking became coercion, and no one on the Court had drawn that line in a way that ended the argument forever.

On Thursday, in Mr. Katz's classroom rearranged into a courtroom, Wyatt stood for the school board. He argued that the school's policy was an invitation, not an order, and when a student justice asked whether the school could not simply leave the pledge alone, Wyatt said, "The school believes some shared ceremonies are worth keeping, even optional ones." Then the sides switched, and he stood for the student and argued that an invitation from a principal is an order wearing nicer clothes, and he watched Mr. Katz write something on his pad without a change in his expression.

Afterward, in the hallway, Isis caught up with him. "Which one did you believe?"

"I don't know yet," Wyatt said. "Both, a little. Barnette says you can't be forced, and I believe that. But the school's side isn't nothing either."

"You're allowed to not know," Isis said. "That's sort of the whole point of the class."

Mr. Katz stopped beside them on his way out, holding his notes against his chest. "Wyatt, your rebuttal for the student was the strongest thing you did. But your closing for the board was the most honest."

"How can the weaker argument be the more honest one?" Wyatt asked.

"Because you argued it like someone who wanted it to be true," Mr. Katz said, "and then you argued against it like someone who understood why it wasn't." He nodded to them both and pushed open the door to the parking lot.

Isis nudged Wyatt's elbow. "You'll get the detractors either way."

"I know," Wyatt said, and pulled his phone out to text his mother that he was walking home.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: On a lead sheet, chord symbols such as C, Am or G7 are written above the staff to show which chord accompanies each part of the melody.
story:
The church basement smelled of damp hymnals and old coffee, and Brayden had claimed the corner table by the radiator because it was the only one that didn't wobble. He spread out his staff paper, sixteen empty bars waiting for him like sixteen unfurnished rooms. Ms. Marino had assigned it for the youth ensemble: a melody, written in standard notation, that Lucius could actually play off the page. Fourteen of the sixteen bars were done. The last two kept coming out sounding like a doorbell.

"You're hovering," said Lucius, dropping into the chair across from him with a binder of piano music under his arm. "Composers who hover over their own pages make me nervous. It's like watching a guy argue with his sandwich."

"I'm not hovering. I'm assessing." Brayden put his pencil down anyway. "The melody's fine. It's the accompaniment I can't figure out. You'd have to improvise under it, and last time you improvised under my stuff you played, and I quote, 'whatever.'"

"Whatever is a legitimate style." Lucius flipped the binder open to a lead sheet, a jazz tune his uncle had given him, and spun it toward Brayden. "Look how they do it here."

Brayden looked. Above the staff, at irregular intervals, floated letters and letter clusters: C, Am, G7, F. Some sat above the first measure, some halfway through a measure, some crowded together over a single beat. Below them, the melody went on its single-minded way, apparently unbothered. He leaned closer, tilting the page toward the lamp. "Wait. So on this kind of sheet, the chord symbols are written above the staff. Like, literally above the exact notes they go with?"

"That's the whole system," Lucius said. "I read the melody, I see C over that part, I play some version of a C chord under it. That's how I accompany you without reading your mind. Which is good, because your mind is a scary place."

Brayden laughed, then went quiet, because his brain had started doing the thing it did in physics class when an equation suddenly described something real. On a lead sheet, chord symbols like C, Am or G7 were written above the staff to show which chord accompanied each part of the melody. Which meant he didn't have to write out Lucius's part at all. He just had to decide, himself, what harmony each piece of his tune belonged to, and write that decision above the right notes, and trust Lucius to build the rest. It was like labeling rooms instead of furnishing them.

Jakub arrived late, as always, shaking rain off his jacket and carrying, inexplicably, a single daffodil. "Don't ask," he said, and sat down. He was the most taciturn of them, a boy who could go an entire rehearsal without ten words, but he had perfect pitch and no patience for music that dodged. He leaned over Brayden's fourteen finished bars and hummed them, straight through, no expression. Then he hummed bar nine again. Then again.

"What," Brayden said.

"Bar nine is lonely," Jakub said, and pointed at the empty air above the staff. "You wrote a note that wants company and then left the party."

That was as close to a lecture as Jakub ever got, and Brayden took it seriously, because Jakub didn't litigate small things. When he had an opinion, it arrived finished. Brayden played bar nine on the upright piano against the wall, then tried a C under it, then an Am, then an F. The Am made the note sound like it was confiding something. The F made it sound like it was apologizing. He tried the G7 and the note suddenly leaned forward, wanting somewhere to go, which was exactly what he wanted for the bridge.

He wrote Am above bar nine, small and deliberate, and felt a strange responsibility in it. In Sunday school, when he was eight, a teacher had explained reparation as setting something right after a wrong, and Brayden thought of it now without knowing why: these little letters above the staff were a kind of setting right. For two years he'd asked accompanists to guess at his music, to invent harmony in the dark, and called that collaboration. Maybe it had been laziness wearing collaboration's coat. Or maybe, and this was the part he couldn't settle, the guessing had produced better music sometimes, the way an apology you invent yourself can be truer than one dictated to you. He genuinely didn't know. He wrote the chords anyway.

The last two bars, when he came back to them, stopped sounding like a doorbell. The G7 he'd placed two bars from the end pulled the melody toward the final C so naturally that the ending seemed to have been hiding there the whole time, waiting for him to stop shoving and let it be found. Lucius sight-read the whole thing, haltingly, then again with his shoulders loosening, and by the third pass he was adding little rolled tenths in his left hand that Brayden had never written and would never have thought of.

"You know the funny part," Lucius said, playing the last chord and letting it hang in the basement's damp acoustics. "I still don't know what you wanted this to feel like. I just knew what to hold up under it."

Jakub set the daffodil on the piano lid and hummed bar nine one more time.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: The principle called Chekhov's gun, from the playwright Anton Chekhov, holds that anything clearly shown on stage early should matter later in the play.
story:
The community theatre smelled of dust and hot glue, and James had claimed the third row center seat because Ms. Lau said writers should watch their work from where an audience would sit. On the stage, marked out in tape on the sprung floor, was the living room of his childhood: one chair, a small table, and a letter that his mother never opened, still in its envelope, which he had written into the first scene because it was true and because it filled an awkward silence in the script.

"So the letter just sits there," Willyam said from the folding table they used for notes, a pencil behind each ear. "Scene one, she sets it down, and then nothing. Two scenes later the play ends." He tapped the page. "Why does the audience keep looking at it?"

"It's my mother's mail," James said. "Plays don't have to explain everything."

Conor looked up from the script. "There's this thing called Chekhov's gun," he said. "Anything clearly shown on stage early should matter later in the play. Chekhov said if you put a gun on the wall in act one, it has to go off." He shrugged. "Ms. Lau had us read his letters last spring."

James wanted to argue that a letter was not a gun, but the difference felt thinner the longer he held it. The audience would see the envelope. They would wait for it. He knew because he had waited, himself, for three years of dinners, watching it yellow on the shelf beside the good dishes, waiting for his mother to open the letter from the hospital that his father had asked her to read aloud to him before he got sick enough that reading stopped mattering.

Ms. Lau came down the aisle with a thermos of coffee and sat one row behind him, uninvolved the way she was when she wanted a student to find the answer alone. "We table-read in twenty minutes," she said. "Decide what the letter is."

He tried a version where the mother opens it in the final scene, but when he read it aloud the speech he invented for her rang false, generous and forgiving in a way his actual mother had never managed, as if the theatre's munificent lighting could rewrite her. He tried a version where the son burns it, which was dramatic and also a lie, because he had never had the nerve. He sat with his head in his hands while Willyam and Conor moved the chair half a foot left and argued about whether people from their town said "sofa" or "couch."

The truth, he admitted finally, was that the letter mattered precisely because nothing happened to it. His culpability in the family's silence was his own: he had never asked her to open it, because as long as it stayed sealed he could believe it contained something unbearable, and believing that let him sublimate his anger into the tidy grief that everyone praised him for. But a play could not stage an absence. He could not put "nothing happened" on a chair and light it.

At the table read, Willyam took the mother's part and Conor the son's, and James read the stage directions in a flat voice, hearing his own sentences for the first time as sounds rather than intentions. When they reached the end, the son still in the room, the letter still sealed, Willyam lowered his pages. "It's better," he said, "but you cheated. The gun's still on the wall."

"Maybe some guns don't go off," James said. "Maybe that's the whole point of my family."

Conor rocked his chair onto its back legs. "Then the play has to make the audience feel the not-going-off. Right now it just looks like you forgot."

Ms. Lau poured her coffee without comment, and James understood that this, too, was an answer, though not the one he wanted. He walked onto the taped-out living room and stood where his mother would stand, and picked up the prop envelope, and realized he did not know what was inside the real one and never would unless he asked, tonight or some night, and that the asking might cost him the story he had already written. The stage lights hummed above him. He put the envelope back on the table, face down, and got out his pencil.
